PRELIMINARY STUDY (De architectura, 4.1.4-6) Ionic order embodies the symbolism of the spiral and the numbers 8 and 5, closely associated with the movement of the planet Venus in antiquity. The Corinthian order, for its part, represents a more elaborate and ornate synthesis of the two previous orders, constituting a formal culmination linked to the idea of light and spiritual elevation, frequently interpreted as a symbol of immortality. The Corinthian order is the last of the three classical Greek orders and developed during the 4th century BC. It takes its name from the city of Corinth. The oldest known example is found in the Temple of Apollo Epicurius at Bassae (Arcadia), dating from between 450 and 420 BCE. It is not the main order of the temple — which features an exterior Doric colonnade and an interior Ionic one — but appears exceptionally within the cella.72 On the Corinthian order Vitruvius describes the Corinthian order as one that imitates the slenderness of a maiden, for its form evokes the most delicate and graceful adornments of a young woman in the bloom of her youth: “The third style, called Corinthian, imitates virginal slenderness, because its form recalls the most beautiful adornments of a maiden, depicted with the most slender limbs due to her tender age. It is said that the discovery of this capital occurred thus: a maiden of Corinth, already of marriageable age, fell ill and died. Her nurse gathered the toys with which the girl used to play in life, placed them in a small basket, and, taking it to her tomb, placed it upon her. To protect these objects from the open air, she covered the basket with a tile. By chance, this basket fell upon an acanthus root. When spring arrived, the acanthus root, pressed by the weight, sprouted leaves and stems which, as they grew along the sides of the basket and met the edges of the tile, bent outwards, forming volutes. ” Explanatory note — Bk. 4.1 (origin of the Corinthian capital). Vitruvius credits the invention of the Corinthian capital to the sculptor Callimachus, active in Athens and Corinth in the later fifth century BC. The Athenians 72It was created as a representation of the cult of Apollo-Asclepius. It can be interpreted as the Greek version of the fundamental pillar, also a philosopher 's sun. 111

nicknamed him κατατηξίτεχνος (catatexitechnos), 'one who refines his art to the point of wearing it away,' for the extreme delicacy of his marble carving; some editions abbreviate the word to catatechnos. The aetiological tale —the votive basket on the Corinthian maiden's tomb, the acanthus root, and the volutes formed as the stalks bent against the tile— should be read not as history but as an aition, a foundation myth that turns a natural accident into an artistic canon. In 4.1.9 the objects the girl delighted in while alive render the Latin pauculis ('a few small things,' hence 'playthings'), the reading adopted in this edition against the poculis ('cups') of Rose and the Loeb; both go back to an old hesitation in the tradition, and the funerary context favors the former. The capital's symmetria is fixed in 4.1.11: its height equals the lower diameter of the shaft, and the diagonal of the abacus is twice that height. [The author's personal hermeneutic proposal: reading the acanthus as an emblem of regeneration belongs to symbolic interpretation, not to the Vitruvian text.] Comparative note — IV.1. The story of the Corinthian capital is introduced as an account of invention, prima inventio … memoratur. The reading adopted in this edition is pupulis, as in Krohn’s text, referring to the objects with which the girl had played. Printed variants and different interpretations belong in the apparatus. Gros’s commentary on Book IV, Granger and Rowland–Howe provide distinct philological and architectural perspectives; their interpretations should not be conflated with the evidence of an individual manuscript. The account’s aetiological character remains separate from the archaeological history of Corinthian capitals. (De architectura, 4.1.8-9) One of the most unique characteristics of the Corinthian order is its extraordinary slenderness, usually reaching a proportion of 10 diameters in height. In the Greek Archaic period, the worship of celestial deities or archetypes in the form of votive columns was common. These columns often culminated in a bust or appeared as simple pilasters or piles of stones, as in the case of the cult of Hermes. The name of the god Hermes derives from the Greek term herma (ἕρμα), meaning " stone " or " pillar. " Many of the deities later worshipped throughout the rest of Greece and Europe — such as Hermes (Mercury to the 112

PRELIMINARY STUDY Romans), Iris, and Pan — originated in the region of Arcadia, considered the " cradle of the gods. " Interestingly, the name Arcadia (Ἀρκαδία) can be etymologically linked to the concept of arkhé (ἀρχή), meaning principle or origin, evoking the idea of " place of the beginning " or " first cause. " A remarkable testament to the origins of the Corinthian order is the capital found in the circular foundations of the Tholos of Epidaurus, carefully buried in antiquity. Its magnificent state of preservation and enigmatic location have led researchers to interpret that it was intentionally placed there by a sculptor as a model for future generations of stonemasons. This example, the oldest known Corinthian capital, is currently housed in the Archaeological Museum of Epidaurus.73 On the Corinthian order and its possible symbolic meaning The author proposes a symbolic association between the Corinthian order and the cultic spheres of Apollo and Asclepius, deities connected with healing and renewal. The early Corinthian column inside the Temple of Apollo Epicurius at Bassae provides a relevant comparison. Its presence does not, by itself, establish the order’s origin in an Apollonian healing cult. According to the account transmitted by Vitruvius (De architectura 4.1.8-9), the Corinthian capital was invented by the sculptor and architect Callimachus. The anecdote relates that, beside the tomb of a young Corinthian woman, a nurse placed a basket containing the deceased's toys and covered it with a square tile for protection. An acanthus root, growing beneath the basket, sent its leaves sprouting through the mesh, curving gracefully under the weight of the tile and giving rise to the characteristic shape of the Corinthian capital. This narrative, which survives only in Vitruvius's treatise, constitutes the best-known legendary explanation for the origin of the architectural order. In the symbolic reading proposed here, the Corinthian column is compared with arboreal imagery associated with Apollo. The acanthus basket, ascending stems, and curling foliage invite an interpretation in terms of growth, renewal, 73Tholos (θόλος; plural tholoi) denotes a building of circular plan in Greek architecture. Historians also apply the term to certain circular or corbel-vaulted funerary structures, whose functions and dates vary. It should not be restricted to a single architectural type or period. 113

and healing. This comparison concerns the reception and meaning of the form; it does not establish descent from a particular ancient tree cult. This interpretation finds a certain parallel in the eastward expansion of the Corinthian style. During the Hellenistic and Roman periods, the order spread across vast regions of the Indo-European world, reaching as far as Gandhara (present-day northern Pakistan and Afghanistan). In this cultural context, Corinthian columns were adapted locally and sometimes crowned with images of Buddha instead of the traditional acanthus flower, merging the classical Mediterranean form with Buddhist iconography.74 The Corinthian capital, the most elaborate of the three classical orders, is characterized by its plant basket shape composed of acanthus leaves, from which volutes and cauliculi emerge that support the abacus. Hymns to Apollo Callimachus, Hymn IV to Delos75 “You did not fear the wrath of Hera, who raged terribly against the mortals who gave birth to Zeus’s offspring, and especially against Leto, the only goddess destined to conceive a son more beloved by the Father than Ares. From the ether, the goddess watched in person, consumed by boundless anger … Arcadia fled from her, and the sacred mountain of Augea turned away from her.” Critical note: The passage describes Leto's wanderings throughout Greece due to Hera's curse, which forbade her from finding refuge on the mainland. The geographically detailed escape (Arcadia, Mount Augeas) is a typical feature of Callimachus's scholarship. The Hamadryads and Apollo's Premonition (vv. 80-100 approx.) “The nymphs rejoice when the rain makes the oak trees grow; the nymphs, on the other hand, weep when the oak trees lose their leaves.¹ Against them Apollo, still contained in the maternal womb, was greatly indignant and inflicted this threat, which would not remain in vain, against Thebes: “Thebes! Why, wretched one, do you defy your fate? Do not force me to prophesy against my will. The seat of the tripod on Pytho is not yet mine, nor has the great serpent died; still the monster with fearsome jaws crawls from the rock of Pleisto and inspires terror on snowy Parnassus, encircling it with the nine rings of its tail. With absolute clarity I announce it to you, with sharper clarity than if I spoke from the laurel: flee! For I will soon overtake you to wash my weapons in your blood, since the children of a proud woman have fallen to you. You will not be my nurse, nor will Cithaeron. I am pure, and only those who are pure will I pity. ” II. The birth of Leto (vv. 205–210 approx.) “Leto untied her belt and leaned her back against the trunk of a palm tree.⁴ A cold sweat ran down her body; exhausted, she finally exclaimed: " Why, my son, do you grieve your mother? Behold, beloved son, this is the island that sails upon the sea: be born, my son, be born, and spring forth sweetly from my womb! " III. The song of the swans (vv. 250–255 approx.) “The goddess spoke, and the swans, singers of the god, leaving the Maeonian Pactolus, circled seven times around Delos. With their melodies they lulled the birth, for they are the birds of the Muses, the most melodious of the heavens. For this reason, the child later endowed the lyre with seven strings, as many times as the swans sang of the birth. They did not sing an eighth song, for at that very moment the god emerged into the light. ” Critical and philological notes 1. The Nymphs and the Trees (Hamadryads): The original text refers specifically to the Hamadryads (nymphs whose fate is biologically and temporally linked to a specific tree). The Greek term usually used by Callimachus is drys, which strictly designates the holm oak or oak, not the generic "tree. " The temporal correspondence of their lives is a classic motif in Hellenistic poetry. 115

2. The restitution of Plisto for Plinto: The original text provided contained a geographical corruption: it read " Plinth. " Philologically, the correct reading is Plisto or Pleisto (the river or valley at the foot of Parnassus, near Delphi, from where the serpent Python emerges: "...apo Plistoio..."). 3. The talkative/arrogant woman: The allusion to "the talkative woman" (lálos) is a direct reference to Niobe, the daughter of Tantalus, whose hubris (arrogance) in boasting of having more children than Leto caused Apollo and Artemis to massacre all her offspring in Thebes. The precise academic term is pride or impiety. 4. The palm tree of Delos: A fundamental element of Apollonian iconography. Leto gives birth while clinging to the sacred palm tree (phoenix) of the island of Delos (formerly called Asteria, the floating island). 5. The meter of the swans and the lyre: This passage from Callimachus is a mythical etymology of the heptatonic scale. The Greek text emphasizes the exact synchronicity between the seven turns of the swans (kyknoi) and the subsequent structure of Apollo's lyre. Euripides, Ion7677 “O blessed Nike! ¹ Come to the Pythian palace, descending in swift flight from the peaks of Olympus to the chambers where Phoebus dwells. There, on the Omphalos², the sacred navel that is the center of the earth, and beside the tripod revered by the choruses, the god proclaims his infallible oracles. ” Critical Notes 1. Nike and Athena: In this chorus of Ion, the supplicants invoke Athena Nike (Victory) and Artemis to intercede for the fertility of Xuthus and Creusa. The use of the term blessed (potnia/ makaira) is a direct ritual epithet. 2. The Omphalos and the Tripod: The original Greek text contrasts the fixity of the Omphalos (ὀμφαλός) — the geometric and sacred center of the 76Euripides (Εὐριπίδης; c. 480–406 BCE) was one of the principal tragic dramatists of classical Athens, alongside Aeschylus and Sophocles. 77Pausanias describes the Delphic omphalos and records the tradition that located the center of the earth there. Philological translation and restitution Critical Notes for the Exegetical Apparatus 1. The invocation and the pain (Apollon, Apollon): The original text is not a lyrical apologia to the "beautiful Sun" in a celebratory sense; it is a cry of sacred terror. Cassandra invokes the god of light on the threshold of death. The confusion with the "Sun" (Helios) stems from the late Hellenistic assimilation (common in Euripides ' treatment of the god in tragedies such as Phaethon), where sunlight is directly associated with Apollo's destructive rays. The epithet Agyieus (Ἀγυιεύς): In the original Greek, the text alludes to Apollo Agyieus, the protector of streets, entrances, and gates. In front of the palace of Mycenae stood a conical pillar or baetylus representing the god. For the prophetess, however, this pillar is no longer a symbol of architectural protection; instead, it has become the boundary marker that delimits the space where she will be sacrificed. The philological core: the mythical etymology (Apóllymi): This passage contains one of the most famous etymological puns in Greek tragedy. There is a deliberate homophony between the name of the god Apollo (Ἀπόλλων) and the verb ἀπόλλυμι (apóllymi), which means “to destroy,” “to annihilate,” “to ruin,” or “to kill.” When the text declares that “mortals rightly call you Apollo,” it enacts a linguistic revelation: the god of harmony and order is, for the one who suffers his severity, “The Destroyer.” The basilica of Ordona The Basilica of Ordona (ancient Herdonia, in Apulia, Italy), erected during the reign of Emperor Augustus at the end of the 1st century BC, is one of the most significant archaeological examples for the study of the Roman basilica typology. In architectural historiography, this building is analyzed in close 123

parallel with the famous Basilica of Fanum Fortunae (Fano), the only structure that Vitruvius himself claims to have built in the Colonia Julia Fanestris and which he meticulously described in Book V of his treatise De architectura. Although the Basilica of Ordona is currently in ruins, its epigraphic and monumental remains allow us to study the materialization of the imperial canon. As with Vitruvius's testimony regarding Fanum — where the architect acknowledges having altered the symmetrical proportions of the theoretical model to adapt to the existing conditions and needs of the forum — the basilica of Ordona demonstrates a clear architectural adaptation to the topographical characteristics of the terrain and the pre-existing urban layout. Addendum (2026, preliminary data): The archaeological discovery of the Fano basilica. For centuries, the basilica of Fanum Fortunae existed only in the words of Vitruvius himself (De architectura 5.1.6-10), the only work the author claims to have personally designed and directed. In January 2026, however, preventive excavations associated with the renovation of Piazza Andrea Costa in Fano, as part of a project funded by the Italian National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), unearthed the remains of a large public building whose plan, proportions, and colonnade remarkably match Vitruvius's description. The Superintendence of Archaeology, Fine Arts and Landscape of Ancona and Pesaro-Urbino, together with the Vitruvian Studies Center and the Polytechnic University of Marche (P. Clini), announced the identification: the excavated remains occupy, on site, approximately 50 by 35 meters — a provisional figure, pending the completion of the dig — with a rectangular floor plan and a perimeter colonnade, and one of its columns, reconstructed from its diameter, would measure about 1.47 meters—approximately the five Roman feet that Vitruvius prescribed for the columns of his basilica. Critical and historiographical notes Geographical clarification (Fano vs. Ordona): It is vital to disentangle the claim that Vitruvius's basilica was built in Ordona. Vitruvius was explicit: his basilica was in Fanum Fortunae. Ordona's significance lies in the fact that its Augustan basilica is contemporary with Vitruvius's writings and demonstrates how the plan model with an internal colonnade and tribunal was becoming standardized in Roman Italy. 125

3. Chronology. Augustus ruled from 27 BCE to 14 CE. Vitruvius’s activity belongs to the late Republic and the early Augustan period; this context does not establish an exact date for every building discussed in the treatise.90 The basilica at Fanum Fortunae is described by Vitruvius as a building he designed and supervised (5.1.6–10). Its reconstruction has long been debated through comparison with the text and other Roman basilicas. On 19 January 2026, the Italian Ministry of Culture announced the identification of the remains in Piazza Andrea Costa, Fano, as Vitruvius’s basilica. That institutional identification must be distinguished from the continuing excavation, the full publication of the evidence and the assumptions embodied in modern reconstructions. Located directly adjacent to the forum, a proportional reconstruction from the sesquialtera (3:2) ratio prescribed by Vitruvius himself yields a basilica of about 144 by 96 Roman feet (approximately 42.65 by 28.43 meters); this idealised modular figure should be distinguished from the provisional on-site measurement of the excavated remains noted above. The architectural program also incorporates an internal peristyle of thirty-two tubular columns. However, archaeological evidence and the literary passage itself reveal a substantial divergence from the theoretical basilica model: the integration of an Aedes Augusti, or temple dedicated to the imperial cult, into its rear flank. This insertion altered the traditional axial symmetry of the Roman building by displacing the classical tribunal, demonstrating that the material execution of the cubus and the architectural order was flexibly adapted to the demands of the terrain's topography and the pre-existing political and religious conditions of the urban space. Vitruvius breaks the regularity of the central colonnade to open an exedrae space in front of the emperor's temple, thus uniting the civil function (basilica) with the sacralization of the State (imperial cult). Latin word fanum properly designates the "sacred place" or the "sanctuary" consecrated to a deity. From this root derives the adjective fanaticus, a term that originally referred to a temple servant or one who manifested an ecstatic enthusiasm provoked by the proximity of the deity; it was only with historical development that the word acquired the pejorative connotation of intransigence that it retains today. In contrast, everything that remained outside the walls of the sacred precinct was called pro-fanum, the direct origin of the modern concept of "profane," which delimits the realm of the secular from the sacred. Beyond the biographical outlines of Marcus Vitruvius Pollio — scarce, fragmentary, and difficult to verify historiographically — this study focuses on his crucial theoretical and practical contributions to the field of architecture. His treatise exerted a decisive influence on construction practices and architectural writing from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance, maintaining an undeniable epistemological relevance. To understand the scope of his work, it is essential to contextualize the author within the late Republic and the early Principate of Rome, a chronological arc spanning the dictatorships of Julius Caesar (49–44 BCE) and the reign of Octavian Augustus (27 BCE– 14 CE). It should be noted that, within the catalog of Roman-era structures that survive today, no epigraphic or archaeological documentation remains that would allow any work to be formally attributed to him. The only exception to this monumental void would be the Basilica of Fanum Fortunae (Fano), in northern Italy; in Book V of his treatise De architectura, Vitruvius himself offers a detailed description of a basilica of his own design built in that colony. Although architectural historiography often establishes fruitful formal parallels between this Vitruvian model and the Basilica of Ordona (in Apulia), it must be clarified that in the current archaeological record of Fano, no substructural remains have 127

been found that coincide unequivocally with the literal description given in the treatise. Critical Notes 1. Clarification of the concept Fanaticus: The redefinition of the term cleanses the text of a modern sociological interpretation ("sacralizing everyday life") and restores it to its true Roman religious origin: the fury of the priests of the temples (fana). 2. Fano and Ordona should not be confused. The basilica at Herdonia (Ordona, in Apulia) is adduced here only as a typological parallel for the study of the Roman basilica; the basilica that Vitruvius states he designed and built (De architectura 5.1.6–10) stood at Fanum Fortunae (Fano), and nowhere else. The recent excavations at Fano remain under study, and the identification, though promising, is not yet certain. 3. Unification of chronology: The temporal indication of the transition from Republic to Empire has been refined using the precise historical concepts of Roman historiography: the end of the Republic and the beginning of the Principate. “In Book V of De architectura, Vitruvius establishes the modular coordinates that should govern the plan of the forensic basilica, determining that the harmonic ratio between its length and width should range between a maximum of 3:1 and a minimum of 2:1. Immediately after establishing this theoretical framework, the author introduces the description of the Basilica of Fano as an advanced design paradigm that subverts and refines these very rules. In this project, Vitruvius assumes an operational role that transcends mere theoretical speculation, directly involving himself as the architect in charge and supervisor of the construction; this is attested to by his own first-person statement: ‘conlocavi curavique faciendam ’ (“I myself awarded the contract and saw to its execution”).”¹ This personal involvement makes the passage the only autograph testimony where the author confronts his canonical principles with the vicissitudes and material contingencies of the actual work”. Far from constituting an anomaly, this dense and integrated spatial configuration became a fully typified typological constant during the principate of Augustus. However, the true discontinuity of Fano with respect to the preceding republican models lies in the bold assimilation of new prerogatives of a political-ideological nature. Vitruvius describes the insertion of an apse with a semicircular curvature arranged on the axis of one of the longer sides of the building, axially facing the main entrance; This exedrate space housed the tribunal and was formally consecrated as Aedes Augusti, thus becoming the monumental nucleus of the imperial cult within the basilica's civil space. the viewer perceives the colonnade not as an endless corridor, but as a unified and centralized enclosure. 2. The Aedes Augusti as an axial rupture: Traditionally, the tribunals of basilicas were located on the short sides (longitudinal axis). By shifting the apse of the tribunal to the center of one of the long sides (transverse axis) and merging it with the Aedes Augusti, Vitruvius completely alters the flow of movement and the citizen's perspective. The civic building becomes a visual propaganda apparatus: upon entering, the first thing one encounters is the statue or altar of the emperor. “Through the meticulous description of this Aedes Augusti, Vitruvius holds the historiographical merit of having codified the semantic function of the monumental apse in close symbiosis with the civil basilica, configuring a space of strong ideological charge that projects the imperial auctoritas and disseminates a profoundly innovative typological program through the architecture of the State.” As for his treatise De architectura, written and dedicated specifically to the Emperor Augustus, its value transcends its immeasurable subsequent influence; its exceptional status lies in being the only theoretical corpus of architectural tradition from classical antiquity that has survived intact to this day. Rigorously structured in ten books, the treatise addresses in its Book I the very ontology of the discipline, postulating the celebrated triad upon which constructive practice rests: firmitas (structural solidity), utilitas (spatial functionality), and venustas (beauty and eurhythmy). While successive volumes are devoted to the science of materials (Book II) or to the morphology and arrangement of the temples of the immortal gods (Book III), the text is not limited to mere technical prescription, but rises to a profound philosophical speculation on cosmic symmetry, musical harmony, and anthropomorphic modulation. Vitruvius summarizes this theory of the cosmic - human analogy with famous words: " For no building can have a sense of composition without symmetry and proportion, unless it has an exact proportion like that of the limbs of a wellshaped man."¹ (“For no temple can possess an ordered compositional structure without symmetry and proportion—that is, unless it maintains an exact modular analogy with the members of a harmoniously configured human body”).» 130

PRELIMINARY STUDY Critical notes 1. Clarification of the term Rationem (Analogy /Reason): In Vitruvian Latin, ratio is not simply an abstract mathematical "reason "; it is the method of calculation and the internal logic that unifies the parts with the whole. When translated in the context of sacred geometry, the more precise terms are modular analogy or geometric concordance. 2. The Vitruvian triad: It is essential to maintain the Latin terms in italics (firmitas, utilitas, venustas) to preserve the rigor of the theoretical framework. Within the context of this edition, venustas is not superficial ornamentation, but rather the mathematical result of applying the symmetry of the human body and musical consonances to the building plan. 3. The human body as the matrix of space: The final quote is the foundation of the Vitruvian Man theory; this demonstrates that the Roman temple is not an isolated object, but a microcosm: Apollonian architecture takes the perfect measurements fixed by nature in the human body and transfers them to stone using the ruler and compass. In Vitruvius’s metrological account, parts of the human body provide units related by proportion. The finger, digitus, is the smallest of the units listed here. Four fingers make a palm, palmus, and four palms make a foot, pes. The Roman foot therefore contains sixteen fingers. The reception of Vitruvius’s anthropometric canon raises questions about the relation between textual ratios and observed anatomy. In 3.1.2, Vitruvius distinguishes the distance from the upper chest to the hairline, one-sixth of the total height, from the distance to the crown, one-quarter. These endpoints must not be conflated. Leonardo’s accompanying notes give the foot as one-seventh of the body’s height, rather than Vitruvius’s one-sixth; his drawing should therefore be studied as an independent investigation as well as a response to the ancient text. Encyclopedic program in Book X, devoted to civil mechanical engineering and siege warfare or military weaponry. Among the devices described, the vertical wheel and paddle watermill stands out for its incalculable socioeconomic significance, its technological diffusion shaping milling in Western Europe and, later, in the Americas. 131

Architecture and the column as a reflection of the human body The fundamental postulate of Vitruvius's treatises lies in the fact that architectural structures should be designed according to the same laws of symmetry and proportion that govern the " body of a well-formed man " (De architectura, III, 1, 1). This analogical correspondence finds its highest material expression in the evolution of the classical orders, where the column is not conceived as a mere tectonic support, but as a direct anthropomorphic transposition: the Doric column embodies the robustness, proportion, and strength of the male body, while the Ionic and Corinthian columns translate the slenderness, delicacy, and ornamentation associated with the female physiognomy. Critical Notes 1. Roman metrology. In the Roman system of measurement, the palmus was not equivalent to a finger (digitus). Rather, the standard relationship was: one pes (Roman foot) equalled four palmi (palms) or sixteen digiti (fingers). Consequently, one palmus corresponded to four digiti. Textual and Metrological Note 2. The precision of Ortiz y Sanz: The Spanish neoclassical academic José Ortiz y Sanz (1787) made a rationalist critique of Vitruvius based on the dissection and observation of real bodies, marking the Enlightenment's break with the blind acceptance of ancient texts. 3. Leonardo’s construction uses two centers: the navel for the circle and a point near the groin for the square. Vitruvius explicitly identifies the navel as the center of the circle and equates the span of the arms with bodily height. He does not require the two figures to share a single center. Leonardo’s drawing is therefore an interpretation of the transmitted instructions; the difference between its centers does not by itself demonstrate that the Latin text was geometrically mistaken. 93Among the early attempts at graphic reconstruction of the Basilica of Fano, the seminal contribution of Fra Giocondo stands out, author 94of the first illustrated edition of Vitruvius's work in 1511. Giocondo's reconstruction 93 The peristasis, whose name comes from the Greek "περίστασις" which means "space around," refers to a colonnaded portico that surrounds the cella of a peripteral temple, common in both the architecture of Ancient Greece and that of Roman temples. 132

PRELIMINARY STUDY focuses primarily on the development of the floor plan, adopting a rigorous 2:1 modular ratio between its length and width. According to his interpretation, the building's internal colonnade was articulated by an arrangement of four columns on its shorter sides, eight in the intercolumniation of the long northern side, and six on the southern side. In this layout, the North wall incorporated a notable axial opening aligned with the Aedes Augusti; Fra Giocondo conceived the latter not as an integrated exedra, but as a freestanding and independent architectural structure, formalized according to the typology of a rectangular peripteral temple. However, the humanist substantially altered the Vitruvian text by shifting the apse of the tribunal towards one of the short sides of the basilica, contravening the explicit transverse location (on the long side) prescribed by the Latin treatise writer; a conscious amendment that reflects the theoretical debates of the architectural synod of the 16th century in the face of the apparent inconsistencies of the original manuscript. In contrast to Giocondo's proposal, the critical edition and commentaries of Daniele Barbaro (1556) —enriched with the masterful engravings of Andrea Palladio — offered a philological solution more faithful to the Vitruvian canon. Barbaro's proposal restores the central colonnade, respecting the sesquialter and longitudinal proportions of the space, flanked by an ambulatory or perimeter portico with a span of twenty feet. It also faithfully places the semicircular apse of the tribunal on the symmetrical axis of the longer side, preceded by a pronaos that organically unifies the civic space of the basilica with the sacred precinct of the imperial cult. Critical notes exegetical and bibliographical apparatus 1. Clarifying the error regarding the peristasis: By correcting "external peristasis" to " internal colonnade," the text regains archaeological coherence. Initially a religious figure and teacher, he distinguished himself especially as a scholar dedicated to the study of classical antiquity. Over time, he broadened his interests and became an eminent antiquarian, archaeologist, military engineer, and architect. not a covered forum. What Fra Giocondo depicts is an internal framework of columns to support the double-height roofs (clerestory). 2. The Barbaro-Palladio partnership: In the history of architectural treatises, it is essential to mention that Daniele Barbaro's Commentaries on Vitruvius (published in Venice) cannot be understood without Andrea Palladio's drawings. Palladio was the one who geometrically solved the problem of the Aedes Augusti on the long side, applying for the first time a solution that integrated the triumphal arch into the transept, a discovery he would later apply in his own Venetian churches (such as San Giorgio Maggiore). Daniele Matteo Alvise Barbaro (Venice, February 8, 1514 – ibid., April 13, 1570) was one of the most outstanding figures of Venetian humanism in the 16th century. Although he developed a preeminent ecclesiastical career after being appointed Patriarch-Elect of Aquileia in 1550, his universal renown lies in his multifaceted nature as a scholar, philosopher, mathematician, and art theorist. Barbaro's most significant intellectual legacy lies in architectural treatises and the science of vision. In 1556, he published his monumental I dieci libri dell'architettura di M. Vitruvio, an annotated translation that established the philological standard for Vitruvius's text thanks to his close collaboration with the architect Andrea Palladio. Simultaneously, Barbaro expanded the boundaries of geometric representation in his celebrated treatise La pratica della perspettiva (1568), where he rigorously analyzed the laws of conic projection and anamorphosis. In this field, his empirical experiments with the camera obscura proved pioneering for the history of science, introducing for the first time a biconvex diaphragm to correct chromatic aberrations and optimize the sharpness of the projected image, prefiguring the principles of modern photographic optics. These successive hermeneutical approaches — from Fra Giocondo's pioneering schemes to Barbaro and Palladio's rigorous readings — demonstrate that the reconstruction of the Basilica of Fano has not been a univocal process. On the contrary, the building's restoration has operated as a field of theoretical experimentation throughout the history of architecture, where each designer and philologist has projected their own aesthetic, scientific, and spatial assumptions onto the suggestive gaps in the original text. 134

Aurelius, Publius Numisius, and Gnaeus Cornelius. The scholar and intellectual Berardo Galiani, in his influential 18th-century critical edition, identified this circle of collaborators as citizens originally from Formia, a solid prosopographical correlation that has served to support the hypothesis of the author's own birth in that town in Campania." This conjecture finds significant archaeological support in the figure of Publius Numisius, the architect whose documented authorship includes the monumental theater of Herculaneum. Architectural historiography has revealed remarkable typological and structural parallels between this Herculaneum building and the Roman Theater of Formia, suggesting the existence of a regional school or building tradition shared by Numisius and Vitruvius. Furthermore, Vitruvius's text reveals a profound geographical and technical familiarity with the southern Latium region, manifested in his precise descriptions of the Pontine Marshes and the physicochemical properties of the thermal waters of Terracina (Neptune's spring). This topographical proximity is further reinforced by his mention of prominent figures from the local aristocracy and late Roman intellectual circles, such as Marcus Terentius Varro and Licinius Murena, whose property holdings and influence in the Gulf of Gaeta area strengthen Vitruvius's place within the social fabric of the Formia elite. Equally revealing is the episode linking the architect to the retinue of Gaius Julius, son of Masinissa¹, the celebrated Numidian monarch. This international contact not only illustrates Vitruvius's high technical status within the Caesarian administration, but also demonstrates the integration of Roman engineers into the diplomacy and high politics of the Neo- Hellenistic Mediterranean. Although the debate surrounding Vitruvius's birthplace remains open within the discipline, with historical candidates such as Verona, Fano, or Fondi alternating, the density of epigraphic and geographical evidence linked to Formia lends this hypothesis a high degree of scientific plausibility, shaping the human backdrop from which the universal knowledge compiled in De architectura would be projected. 136

Allegory of the duplication of the cube Editorial note. — This allegory likewise forms part of the editor’s interpretive perspective. The Delian problem of doubling the cube appears in Vitruvius (IX, pref. 13–14) as a historical anecdote; the allegorical and symbolic reading proposed here is the editor’s own and carries no philological authority. “Following the devastating health crisis that ravaged Athens during the Peloponnesian War, and which claimed the life of the statesman Pericles, a delegation of citizens went to the famous Oracle of Apollo on the island of Delos¹ with the purpose of finding a divine remedy to alleviate the plague. The deity's response dictated a condition of strict geometric precision: to appease divine wrath, it was imperative to erect a new altar that exactly doubled the volume of the pre-existing one, which had a perfect cubic configuration. The Hellenic geometers, committing an error of linear proportionality, proceeded to double the length of the edges of the original altar, which quadrupled its surface area and exponentially increased its volume eightfold², thus failing to solve the enigma.” Although the epidemic eventually subsided through natural cycles, the mathematical challenge survived as a profound allegory about the inadequacy of elementary arithmetic in the face of the complexity of threedimensional space. This episode, recorded in the doxographical tradition by authors such as Eratosthenes of Cyrene and Plutarch, transcends mere historical anecdote to become the birth certificate of the "Delian problem."³ Apollo's demand was not a mere ritual whim, but a subtle theoretical reproach to the Greeks for their neglect of the geometry of solids, prompting mathematicians of the stature of Hippocrates of Chios, Archytas of Tarentum, and Plato to explore the properties of proportional lines and lay the foundations of the sacred geometry of perfect volumes.95 95The Oracle of Delphi, in the Sanctuary of Delphi, was a place for consulting the gods, in the sacred temple dedicated primarily to the god Apollo. Located in Greece, in the present-day town of Delphi, at the foot of Mount Parnassus, consecrated to the god himself and the Muses, amidst the mountains of Phocis, at 700 meters above sea level. m above sea level and 9.5 km away from the Gulf of Corinth. 140

PRELIMINARY STUDY notes for the exegetical and mathematical apparatus 1. Delos and Delphi. The mathematical tradition associates the doubling of a cubic altar with the Delian problem. The story of Apollo’s killing of Python belongs to the Delphic cycle. Neither the mathematical legend nor a symbolic comparison establishes the physical form of a particular surviving altar. 2. geometric error: If the original altar has a side s, its volume is V₁ = s³. By mistakenly doubling the side (2s), the new volume turns out to be: V₂ = (2s)³ = 8s³ The Athenians multiplied the volume by eight instead of by two. To exactly double the volume (V₂ = 2V₁), the new edge should have measured s · ∛2, an irrational number whose geometric construction was impossible using only the traditional straightedge and compass. 3. The Platonic interpretation of the myth: According to Plutarch (De E apud Delphi), when the Athenians turned to Plato to solve the problem of the oracle, the philosopher of the Academy replied that Apollo did not need a double altar, but used the pretext of the altar to force the Greeks to abandon political and commercial disputes and dedicate themselves to the study of high geometry, the only discipline capable of purifying the intellect and attuning it to the order of the cosmos. The traditions should be distinguished. The death of Python belongs to the Delphic cycle of Apollo. The problem of doubling the cube is associated with an oracle at Delos, hence the name “Delian problem”. A connection between the two may be explored as an interpretation, but should not be presented as a single ancient narrative. “According to the foundational account of the Homeric Hymn to Apollo, a serpentine creature of colossal proportions — associated by the sources with the chthonic powers of Gaia or her daughter Themis — guarded the ancient oracle of Delphi near the Castalian Spring. The sacred text describes it as a beast of unyielding strength, corpulent, enormous wild beast that brought great misfortunes upon men on earth… It was this dragon who welcomed and fed the fierce and tremendous Typhon, nightmare of mortals.”¹ In the exegesis of sacred geometry, this mythical feat runs parallel to the origin of the most celebrated three-dimensional enigma of antiquity: the duplication of the cube, or the Delos problem.² Along with the squaring of the circle and 141

the trisection of the angle, this challenge forms the triad of classical problems in Greek geometry. While modern mathematics has demonstrated the impossibility of solving them using only the ideal ruler and compass³, for ancient thought these dilemmas were not mere axiomatic puzzles, but rather true instruments of theoretical transmutation. They represented states of consciousness and the faculty of deciphering, within allegory, an ontological reality that transcended the written word. To solve them, the geometer needed to undergo a metanoia: to "turn the plane" and approach the archetype from a higher dimension. The first mathematician to formulate an analytical solution to this problem was Hippocrates of Chios (c. 470 – c. 410 BCE). The pre-Socratic geometer discovered that the problem of doubling the cube reduced geometrically to a problem of interpolation: the insertion of two continuous mean proportionals between a given segment and its double. Mathematical and Philological Formalisation In classical notation, and according to the theory of proportions set out in Book VIII of Euclid’s Elements, if an initial segment a and its double 2a are given, and two mean proportionals r and s are inserted between them, the following continued proportion is established: a : r = r : s = s : 2a In modern algebraic notation, this may be expressed as a/r = r/s = s/2a. From these equalities it follows that r² = as and s² = 2ar. Squaring the first equation and substituting the value of s² obtained from the second yields 142

PRELIMINARY STUDY r⁴ = a²s², r⁴ = a²(2ar), r⁴ = 2a³r. Since r ≠ 0, division by r gives r³ = 2a³. Thus the cube constructed on the first mean proportional r has exactly twice the volume of the cube constructed on the original segment a. The celebrated Delian problem — the duplication of the cube — therefore ceased to be a matter of physical conjecture and became a rigorous problem in the theory of mean proportionals. The search for the dimensions of the new Apollonian altar was transformed into a precise mathematical investigation grounded in geometric proportion. Philologically, the designation “Delian altar” is preferable to “Apollonian altar.” Although the tradition associates the episode with an altar of Apollo on the island of Delos, classical and modern scholarship alike have generally referred to the challenge as the Delian Problem (Problema Delium) or *the Duplication of the Cube. The use of “Delian altar” therefore aligns the terminology with the established historiographical and mathematical tradition. Critical Notes 1. The nature of Typhon and Chaos: By shooting arrows at the dragon, Apollo not only cleanses the sanctuary, but also subjects the chaotic fluids of the earth to the fixity of the oracular axis (Omphalos). 2. The Transition from the Second to the Third Dimension: The discovery of Hippocrates of Chios is a methodological stroke of genius. He understood that a solid cannot be duplicated using simple proportions of (twodimensional) surfaces. By requiring two proportional means instead of one (since a single mean, the geometric mean a: r :: r: 2a, serves to duplicate the square, that is, r² = 2a²), Hippocrates forces the elevation from the plane to volume, opening the door to rational three-dimensional geometry. 143

3. Modern mathematical perspective. Wantzel’s result of 1837 establishes that a cube cannot be doubled using straightedge and compass alone, because the cube root of two is not constructible by successive quadratic extensions. This modern proof must not be attributed to ancient geometers. The constructions associated with Archytas and Menaechmus belong to the ancient investigation of the problem by other means. Their association here with light and the material plane is the author’s symbolic interpretation. The first is of a historical - mathematical nature: the solutions of Archytas, Menaechmus, and Eratosthenes were not approximate, but geometrically exact. The misconception lies in the fact that they did not use only a ruler and compass (which is impossible, as modern mathematics has demonstrated), but rather developed advanced mechanical curves and conic sections of absolute precision. The second point of clarification is philological -etymological: the original name of the region was not Pyto, but Pito (from the Greek Pythó, Πυθώ), derived from the verb pythein (to rot), alluding to the body of the serpent defeated by Apollo. “Building on the theoretical framework established by Hippocrates of Chios, other preeminent geometers of antiquity took up the challenge of geometric duplication. Far from proposing empirical approximations or estimated calculations, scientists of the stature of Archytas of Tarentum, Menaechmus, and Eratosthenes of Cyrene formulated solutions of strict geometric accuracy. To overcome the operational limitations of the plane ruler and compass, these authors needed to expand the horizons of the discipline: Archytas integrated the third dimension through a bold constructive model of the intersection of threedimensional solids (a cylinder, a cone, and a torus); Menaechmus discovered conic sections (the parabola and the hyperbola) as spatial cutting tools; and Eratosthenes mechanized the process through a kinematic instrument known as the mesolabe.” Alongside this scientific development, the nerve center of the Apollonian cult, the Oracle of Delphi, stood majestically on the slopes of Mount Parnassus in Phocis. The sanctuary, dedicated to Apollo, was inextricably linked to a sacred landscape where water acted as an agent of purification and prophecy. Among the various springs that dotted the site, the Castalian Spring stood out, its waters flowing flanked by a dense laurel forest, the plant attribute sacred to the god. 144

PRELIMINARY STUDY Mythical tradition celebrated this numinous setting as the meeting place of the Muses, where Apollo's lyre orchestrated the song of the inspired deities. In the context of Archaic and Classical Greece, this sacred site was originally called Pytho, a theonym that evoked the chthonic decomposition of the defeated monster. Over the centuries, linguistic usage assimilated both traditions, and the original toponym of Pito yielded its preeminence to the definitive designation of Delphi. Critical Notes 1. The accuracy of the "mechanical" solutions: In the history of science, it is vital to clarify that the solutions of the Academy and the school of Tarentum were exact. Archytas of Tarentum (c. 428–347 BCE), a friend of Plato, solved the duplication of the cube using a doublecurvature curve that foreshadows modern analytic geometry. Menaechmus (c. 380–320 BCE) demonstrated that the two continuous mean proportionals corresponded to the coordinates where two parabolas, or a parabola and a hyperbola, intersect. To call these solutions "approximate" would weaken the thesis on the regularity of Apollonian geometry. 2. The etymology of Pytho (Pythó): The phonetic change to Pyto should be corrected by its academic spelling: Pito. Philologically, the name connects the physical space with the myth of the serpent's death: Apollo lets the midday sun rot (pythein) the monster's corpse. From this "putrefaction" springs the purification of the earth. The later transition to the name Delphi (Delphoi) is etymologically associated with delphys (womb or matrix), signifying that the sanctuary went from being the place of the dragon's death to becoming the spiritual matrix and the Omphalos (navel) of the Greek world.96 Typhon, in Greek mythology, personified earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. Apollo killed him and let the brilliant Hyperion (the Sun) rot him; in ancient Greek: pytho. Hence the name Pythius, by which the god was also known. 96Delphi (Greek Δελφοί (m. pl.), Ancient Greek Δελφοί pronounced Delphoí), originally called Pytho (Πυθώ), was a city of ancient Greece, best known for its oracle. Both names are synonymous. 145

PRELIMINARY STUDY nevertheless, the geometric intuition is accurate: the plinth represents the square base or cube upon which the order rests. “From this toponym derives the title of Pythia (pythōnissa), the official designation of the priestess who channeled prophecies in the sacred precinct of Delphi. The term Pythō (Pythō) is inextricably linked to Python, the mythical serpentine creature that guarded the buttresses of Mount Parnassus and which Apollo slew to establish his oracular hegemony. According to mythographic tradition, after defeating the monster, the god deposited its ashes in an underground receptacle located immediately beneath the omphalos; it was from this 'navel of the world' that the priestesses assimilated the prophetic vapors emanating from the chthonic entrails to deliver their oracular responses.” In the sacred topography of Hellas, the temple consecrated to this deity was called Pythion (in classical Greek, Πύθιον), and the god himself received the cultic epithet of Apollo Pythius. During the Archaic period, the veneration of Apollo took on a markedly geometric character, being worshipped in the form of a plinth (πλινθός), a term that in classical sources designates both the mud brick and the cubic pedestal. This aniconic form of worship — the sacralization of a pure geometric volume in place of anthropomorphic or figurative representation — is solidly documented in ancient literature and the archaeology of Latium and Greece. In the grammar of the classical architectural orders, the plinth constitutes the smooth, quadrangular element that serves as the base and interface between the column shaft and the stereobate, symbolizing the cubic fixity upon which the verticality of the Doric and Tuscan orders unfolds. Critical Notes 1. Architectural Clarification (Plinth vs. Abacus): It is vital for technical rigor not to confuse the plinth with the abacus. The plinth is at the base of the column (earth, cubic stability). The abacus is at the top, crowning the capital. The plinth, as a "cubic pedestal," acquires perfect coherence with the concept of the cubic altar of Delos: the god of geometry manifests himself at the very base of the structure, in the cubic rooting with matter. 2. The Aniconic Cult and the Cube: The mention of the plinth as a primitive form of Apollo. Authors such as Pausanias document that in Megara and Amyclae, Apollo was worshipped as a bronze column or a quadrangular 149

pillar. This demonstrates that before Greek art humanized the gods (anthropomorphism), the divinity of light and order was expressed through mathematical abstraction. The god is the cube, the straight line, and pure proportion. 3. The Omphalos as a transmuter: The presence of the serpent's ashes under the Omphalos (which was physically a semi-spherical, oconic stone) represents the geometric containment of the forces of chaos. Apollo does not destroy the energy of the earth (the serpent), but rather buries it under an ordered geometric axis (the navel of the world) to transform it into prophecy and rational word (logos). Vitruvius's journey The biographical details of Marcus Vitruvius Pollio remain shrouded in a dense historiographical obscurity; virtually all information about his life comes from passages in his own treatise, De architectura. The determination of his three names is the subject of long-standing philological debates. While the late manuscript tradition consolidated the cognomen "Pollio, " the epigraphic record has opened alternative avenues of research: an inscription found in Verona documents a Lucius Vitruvius Cordo, while another epigraphic evidence in Thibilis (Numidia, North Africa) records the name Marcus Vitruvius Mamurra. This latter coincidence has fueled the intriguing hypothesis of a family relationship, or even a shared identity, between the treatise writer and Mamurra, the celebrated and influential chief engineer (praefectus fabrum) of Julius Caesar. However, none of these attributions finds explicit endorsement in the text of De architectura, a work that the author formally dedicated to Octavian Augustus. On an institutional and professional level, Vitruvius served as a military engineer within the legionary establishment, performing functions similar to those of a praefectus fabrum or an architectus assigned to the armamentarium (the state artillery arsenal). His technical relevance was confirmed in later literature: Pliny the Elder includes him by name in the index auctorum of his Naturalis Historia as an authority on the science of materials and mosaic paving techniques, while Sextus Julius Frontinus, at the end of the 1st century AD, explicitly refers to "Vitruvius the architect" in his treatise De aquaeductu when addressing the standardization of lead pipe modules (fistulae). 150

PRELIMINARY STUDY According to the autobiographical statements in his prefaces, Vitruvius was born into a family of free Roman citizens and pursued his career in the campaigns of the late Republican civil wars. He served in Julius Caesar's artillery forces alongside a select corps of technical officers including Marcus Aurelius, Publius Numisius, and Gnaeus Cornelius. During these campaigns, his geographical postings encompassed various fronts of the Roman Empire: North Africa, Hispania, Pontus, and Gallia Comata (including the regions of Aquitania and Gallia Narbonensis). The nature of the military Apparatio in the Roman army To accurately gauge the operational scope of Vitruvius's rank as a military engineer, historiography frequently turns to the later testimony of Flavius Vegetius Renatus in his Epitoma rei militaris. Vegetius details the vast responsibilities of the praefectus castrorum (camp prefect), a high-ranking officer in charge of the army's construction and logistics: the fortification of the perimeter, the digging of trenches, the organization of tent accommodations, as well as the maintenance and provisioning of siege machinery and transport vehicles. Within this technical framework, Vitruvius specialized in the apparatio tormentorum, that is, the construction and calibration of torsion artillery pieces, primarily ballistae and scorpions, crucial ballistic weapons for siege warfare. Various indications suggest that this training took place under the direct orders of Lucius Cornelius Balbus, the influential praefectus fabrum of Julius Caesar's Gallic campaigns. The precise passages in Vitruvius's treatise analyzing siege mechanics reflect firsthand experience in the major theaters of operations of 52 BCE, such as the fierce siege of Avaricum, the tactical operations before the walls of Gergovia, and finally, the monumental work of circumventing and besieging the stronghold of Alesia. Critical Notes 1. Clarifying the Mamurra Case: The connection between Vitruvius and Mamurra is fascinating. Mamurra was Caesar 's praefectus fabrum in Gaul, famous for his immense wealth and for having introduced the first Carrara marble (marmor lunense) paneling into his palace on the Caelian Hill. If Vitruvius was not Mamurra himself, he undoubtedly belonged to the same technical management. This gives Vitruvius a status far higher than that of a 151

simple soldier: he was a man embedded in the elite of engineering in the Republic. 2. The technical precision of the weapons: Ballistae and scorpions were not calibrated empirically or randomly. In Book X, Vitruvius details how Roman engineers used a mathematical formula based on the weight of the projectile to calculate the diameter of the bore in the bundles of torsion tendons. Roman artillery, therefore, was pure geometry applied to military ballistics. 3. The parallel with Vegetius: Although Vegetius wrote several centuries later (at the end of the Empire), his description of the legions' technical environment confirms that Roman architects were not trained in academies of fine arts, but in the mud of the trenches, surveying the terrain, building palisades, and ensuring the water supply. This is the origin of Vitruvian firmitas: the solidity that must withstand both the ravages of time and the enemy's catapults.97 “Despite his extensive career in military engineering, Vitruvius's enduring legacy lies in his role as a theorist and systematizer of architecture. In the context of ancient Rome, architectura was a discipline of a vastly broader scope than its contemporary counterpart; it encompassed urban planning, construction management and physics, civil and materials engineering, metallurgy, hydrodynamic mechanics, military ballistics, and the science of mechanical devices. This cross-disciplinary nature has led the historiography of technology to recognize Vitruvius as the seminal pioneer of architectural engineering and technical building.” In the field of urban planning and the establishment of settlements, Vitruvius pioneered the integration of Hippocratic medical precepts through miasmatic theory. He maintained that the emanations exhaled by marshy and swampy lands acted as vectors of infectious diseases. When addressing the selection of a site (de electione locorum sanissimorum) for the founding of cities or fortresses, the treatise writer stipulated the obligation to select elevated locations, free from dense fogs and sheltered from extreme climatic fluctuations. He warned with 97Ballista, related to Greek βάλλειν (‘to throw’), denotes an ancient two-armed torsion engine. He also determined that coastal foundations facing south or west suffered from chronic unhealthiness, because continuous sun exposure and thermal stagnation altered the balance of the inhabitants' body humours. Technical Standardization: Hydraulics and Theatrical Acoustics Vitruvius's expertise in the development of public infrastructure was confirmed by Sextus Julius Frontinus, who acknowledged his contribution to the metrological standardization of the diameter of lead pipes (fistulae), a critical advance for the distribution of imperial water resources. Similarly, the historiography of science hails him as the founder of architectural acoustics thanks to his meticulous description of bronze resonating vessels or echeia (ἠχεῖα). These devices, arranged in symmetrical niches beneath the seating tiers of theaters according to strict laws of Pythagorean musical harmony, served to amplify the actors' voices through physical resonance. Although the catalog of his material works remains undocumented, the author left evidence of his direct involvement in the construction of the Basilica of Fanum Fortunae (modern-day Fano), whose erection dates to the first decades of Augustus's reign (c. 27–15 BCE). The material remains of this structure have disappeared from the surface, opening a complex archaeological debate about its exact topographical location. One of the most plausible historiographical hypotheses suggests that, given the recurring early Christian practice of Christianizing civil forum spaces, the substructures and colonnade of the Vitruvian basilica may have been absorbed and integrated into the medieval fabric of the current Romanesque cathedral of Fano. Critical Notes 1. Miasmatic Theory as the Ordering of Chaos: The section on miasmas is vital. Vitruvius demonstrates that the architect not only arranges the stones, but also regulates the invisible elements (air, water, heat). The corrupt air of the swamps represents the chaos of untouched nature; architecture, by choosing the elevated site and laying out the walls, acts as a filter that purifies the environment and allows the Apollonian light and clean air to sustain the life of the citizen. 153

2. The resonating vessels (Echeia) and acoustic harmony: The echeia described in Book V (V, 5) are definitive proof that Vitruvian architecture is solid music. Vitruvius explains that the vessels must be tuned at intervals of a fourth, fifth, and octave. This connects directly with the proportional means of doubling the cube: the Roman theater is not just a building for leisure, but a mathematical instrument designed to attune the vibrations of the human voice to the mathematical harmonies of the cosmos. 3. The syncretism of the Basilica of Fano: The hypothesis that Vitruvius' basilica underlies the cathedral of Fano closes the evolutionary cycle of the building: the civil structure built by Augustus' architect to house the Aedes Augusti (the cult of the emperor) ended up becoming the formal matrix of the Christian temple, demonstrating the perenniality of its geometric axes. In his later years, Emperor Augustus sponsored Vitruvius through his sister Octavia Minor, possibly granting him a pension to ensure his financial independence. The authorship of "De architectura" remains a subject of debate, as it is uncertain whether the text was written by a single author or is a compilation made by later librarians and copyists. The date of Vitruvius's death is unknown, suggesting that he may not have been very popular during his lifetime. Vitruvius's influence and recognition endure to this day. Gerolamo Cardano98, in his 1552 book "De subtilitate rerum," lists him as one of the twelve individuals who, in his view, surpass all others in genius and invention. He might even have placed him first had it been clear that Vitruvius had written down his own discoveries. Furthermore, in James Anderson's "The Constitutions of the Masons" (1734), reprinted by Benjamin Franklin, Vitruvius is considered "the father of all true architects to this day. " In the preface to Book VII, Vitruvius articulates a profound defense of his own intellectual and methodological rigor through one of the first historiographical reviews of ancient scientific literature. By projecting this fear onto his own future, Vitruvius conceives of his treatise not only as a technical manual, but as a documentary monument intended to preserve the universal memory of architecture against the contingency of oblivion. To illustrate the universality and genealogy of knowledge, the author compiles a comprehensive inventory of scientific, philosophical, and artistic authorities. This list, structured in an encyclopedic manner, is broken down into the following critical categories: I. Wise Men of Nature and Thought • Physicists (Physici): Thales of Miletus, Democritus of Abdera, Anaxagoras of Clazomenae and Xenophanes of Colophon. • Philosophers (Philosophi): Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Zeno of Citium and Epicurus. • Monarchs and Patrons (Reges): Croesus of Lydia, Alexander the Great and Darius of Persia. Through this extensive bibliographic apparatus, Vitruvius places his work at the final link in a sacred chain of human knowledge. By indexing these authorities, he demonstrates that architecture is not merely an empirical or manual craft, but a unified science that absorbs physics, geometry, aesthetics, and mechanics, demanding for its practice a profound moral rectitude in the face of the forgetfulness of time. Critical Notes 1. The value of the Preface to Book VII: This text is the first Western "history of architecture." Vitruvius constructs his intellectual family tree here. It is significant that he relates the physics of Thales to the machinery of Archimedes, and the symmetry of Hermogenes demonstrates that all ancient knowledge forms a unified matrix. 2. The Interpolation of Optics (Agatarchus, Democritus, Anaxagoras): The mention of these authors in the section "On Divergence" is crucial. Vitruvius explains that Agatharchus painted a stage set for Aeschylus and left a treatise on how straight lines must curve or diverge to suit the human eye. This demonstrates that Roman sacred geometry was not rigid; architects knew that for a building to appear perfectly cubic or symmetrical to the human eye, they had to apply invisible optical corrections to the actual lines. 3. The legitimization of Cossutius and Mucius: By including Roman architects (Cossutius, Mucius) on the same level as the Greek geniuses Ictinus or Chersiphron, Vitruvius is performing an act of cultural nationalism: he demonstrates that Augustan Rome has reached the technical and artistic maturity necessary to inherit and perfect the geometric canon of the Hellenistic world. It demonstrates that his treatise did not disappear after the first century, but rather that the later imperial administration itself needed to systematize extracts from the text (De 159

To consolidate this crucial chapter on the historiographical fortune of the Vitruvian treatise, it is necessary to specify the technical transition between the Roman world and its humanist rediscovery. From the perspective of the archaeology of construction, the relative silence of Antiquity was not solely due to obscure language, but also to a technological shift: Vitruvius wrote at the dawn of the Principate (still within an architectural tradition rooted in Hellenistic stonework and lintels), just before the great revolution of opus caementicium (Roman concrete) and the monumental vaulted structures that characterized the 1st and 2nd centuries AD (amphitheaters, large baths, and aqueducts supported by arcades). Furthermore, the discovery at Poggio Bracciolini in 1416 was not the only manuscript found, but rather the catalyst for the humanist philology that led to Sulpicius da Veroli's editio princeps and Alberti's creative reinterpretation. " The reception of De architectura in the literature of classical antiquity presents a historiographical paradox: despite being the only theoretical corpus of the discipline preserved in its entirety, its immediate impact on imperial texts was remarkably restricted, limited to the technical mentions of Pliny the Elder, Sextus Julius Frontinus, and the late antique epitome of Cetius Faventinus. This hermeneutical asymmetry is due to stylistic and technical-structural reasons. On the one hand, Vitruvius's prose — characterized by archaic Latin and neological terminology of Hellenistic origin — was difficult to assimilate outside the guilds of the state apparatus. " On the other hand, the treatise was written during the transition from the Republic to the first Empire, a tectonic horizon still anchored in the trabeated orders of Greek origin; because of this, Vitruvius did not systematize the imminent Roman building revolution that would define the following centuries, characterized by the monumental exploitation of opus caementicium, the large tiers of amphitheaters, the development of the engineering of pillars and arches, and the physics of concrete vaults. Despite this retreat in the visual culture of the High Empire, the treatise survived the fragmentation of the West through a robust network of manuscript transmission during the Early and Late Middle Ages. Contemporary philology documents the survival of approximately eighty codices of medieval tradition, 160

PRELIMINARY STUDY among which stand out copies from the Anglo-Saxon and Carolingian eras produced around 800 CE. The preservation of these testimonies in the scriptoria of abbeys and basilica monasteries — such as St. Gallen, Cluny, Canterbury, and Oxford — demonstrates that the Vitruvian text functioned as a repository of Latinity and encyclopedic knowledge, preserving the conceptual framework that would link classical theory with the Renaissance. The advent of Quattrocento humanism radically transformed this scholarly status, elevating Vitruvius to the position of canonical authority for the refounding of constructive practice. The ad fontes movement spurred intellectuals like Poggio Bracciolini to undertake philological research campaigns in monastic libraries; in 1416, Bracciolini unearthed a critical copy of De architectura in the Monastery of St. Gallen, an event that catalyzed the constructive exegesis of the Quattrocento. This process of literary restitution reached its apotheosis with the publication of the editio princeps of the treatise, printed in Rome around 1486 by the humanist Giovanni Sulpicio da Veroli (Sulpicius of Aquila), an event that inaugurated the era of architectural printing and the standardization of European theoretical debate. Hermeneutics and the Genesis of the Modern Treatise Given that medieval manuscripts lacked Vitruvius's original graphic apparatus (the figures mentioned in the text had been lost in the copying process), Renaissance architects were compelled to adopt a methodologically dual approach. The practical application of the ten books demanded a constant dialectical confrontation between the abstract text and the direct examination of the surviving archaeological ruins on Italian soil. Far from being an obstacle, the frequent discrepancies between Vitruvian prescriptions and the materiality of imperial monuments — such as the Colosseum or the Pantheon — opened up a fertile space for interpretive freedom. This hermeneutical gap allowed modern masters to deploy a high degree of creativity and geometric rigor in their spatial design. The Vitruvian influence shaped the foundations of Western architectural theory well into the 19th century. As early as 1452, Leon Battista Alberti completed his De re aedificatoria, a seminal work that adopted the decemviral structure and tripartite conceptual framework of his Roman predecessor, albeit reconfigured through the lens of Platonic philosophy. The expansion of the 161

canon was accelerated by an ambitious program of European vernacular translations, marked by milestones such as the first critical edition in German, published in 1548 by the scholar Walther Hermann Ryff, which consolidated the transalpine universalization of the architectural Sophia of Antiquity. Critical Notes 1. The Fracture of Opus Caementicium: Regarding sacred space and the cube, this point is crucial. Vitruvius defends the use of dressed stone and the traditional Greek static structure because he sees in it an immutable mathematical order. However, later emperors (from Nero with the Domus Aurea to Hadrian with the Pantheon) preferred concrete, a malleable material that allowed them to curve space and create colossal domes. By not addressing these developments, Vitruvius preserved the purity of the straight line and the elemental cubic volume, which is precisely what Alberti and the Renaissance architects inherited to purify sacred space in contrast to the Gothic style. 2. The paradox of the missing figures: It is crucial to emphasize the significance of the absence of illustrations in the text discovered by Poggio Bracciolini. Without drawings, the Renaissance had to imagine proportions through the pure abstract geometry described in the words. Architects like Bramante, Raphael, and Palladio had to rediscover the modular law by reconstructing plans using only ruler and compass, which transformed architecture into a superior mental and mathematical science, detached from the mere medieval craftsmanship of stonemasons. 3. The transition from Vitruvius to Alberti: Leon Battista Alberti did not simply copy Vitruvius; he effected a subtle theoretical transmutation. While the Roman presented an eminently practical vision linked to state engineers, Alberti elevated venustas to the category of Concinnitas (the universal harmony of all parts regulated by absolute mathematical laws, where nothing can be altered without destroying the whole). This is the direct bridge to the hypothesis put forward here: Renaissance architecture takes Vitruvius's military and pragmatic heritage and transforms it into a three-dimensional spatial theology.99 99De re aedificatoria (‘On the Art of Building’) is Leon Battista Alberti’s Latin architectural treatise in ten books, composed around the middle of the fifteenth century. Its critical engagement with Vitruvius made it a foundational text of Renaissance architectural theory. 162

PRELIMINARY STUDY “A key pillar of Vitruvian sacred anthropometry is the theoretical formulation of homo bene figuratus (De architectura, III, 1, 1), a concept that prescribes the intrinsic geometric correspondences of the human body and its precise inscription within the perfect forms of the circle and the square. This microcosmic analogy acted as a powerful catalyst for Renaissance artists and humanists, finding its most celebrated iconic embodiment in Leonardo da Vinci ’s Vitruvian Man (c. 1490). Centuries later, on the horizon of 20th-century modernity, the Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier revived Vitruvian modular methodology through the development of the Modulor (1948).” This system of spatial regulation constituted a harmonic scale that combined the proportions of human physiognomy with the golden section and the mathematical series of Fibonacci, with the purpose of standardizing architectural and industrial production to the measure of man. Regarding the material transmission of the text, contemporary historiography has debunked the myth of the sudden "rediscovery" of Vitruvius by Poggio Bracciolini in 1416 at the Abbey of St. Gall (and not, as a later tradition now discarded claimed, at Montecassino in 1414). Philological research clarifies that Bracciolini unearthed a critical codex of De architectura in the library of the Monastery of St. Gallen in 1416; however, this event did not represent a complete break with the medieval past, but rather the culmination of a latent process of assimilation. Preeminent humanists of the Trecento, such as Francesco Petrarch and Giovanni Boccaccio, had already frequented and annotated Vitruvian manuscripts during the 14th century, demonstrating that the knowledge of Augustus's architect never completely died out in the cultural substratum of pre-Quattrocento Italian intellectuals. Critical Notes 1. Bibliographical correction: The exact translation of Marc van den Broek's work (2018) should appear in the apparatus as: Leonardo da Vinci: The Inventions. A Search for Traces. 2. Vitruvius describes a well-formed human body inscribed in a circle and a square (3.1.3). With the person lying on the back and the limbs extended, compasses placed at the navel trace a circle touching the fingers and toes. The 163

equality of bodily height and arm span supplies the square. Leonardo gives the two constructions distinct centers: the circle at the navel, the square near the groin. The reading of this distinction as a dynamic relation between regulating centers is the author’s interpretive proposal. It does not establish that Leonardo corrected a lost classical drawing. 3. The Petrarch-Boccaccio continuity: Emphasizing that Petrarch read Vitruvius in the 14th century reinforces the theoretical framework regarding the enduring nature of Sophia. Vitruvius was not a "forgotten and resurrected" author, but rather a subterranean presence that silently guided Western aesthetic thought throughout the Middle Ages until it exploded in the Renaissance. Petrarch owned and studied Latin manuscripts of Vitruvius (such as the famous Codex Metropolitanus or its copies in Avignon), making marginal notes (scholia) and commenting on passages in his letters, but the vernacular (Italian) was not used for the translation of this technical treatise until well into the 16th century. “Francesco Petrarch’s intervention in the Vitruvian tradition did not result in a linguistic transposition into Italian, but rather in a work of rescue, collation, and philological exegesis in Latin during the 14th century. Petrarch, considered the herald of Renaissance humanism, located and preserved in his private library manuscript copies of De architectura — at a time when the treatise was considered an extremely opaque text — marking its margins with valuable critical annotations (scholia) that clarified the careless syntax of Imperial technical Latin. His approach to the architect of Augustus was literary and archaeological in nature, motivated by his desire to reconstruct the topography and monumental glories of classical Rome, thus establishing the method that the humanists of the Quattrocento would inherit.” The history of vernacular reception includes manuscript translations as well as print. Cesariano’s Como edition of 1521 was the first printed Italian translation, distinguished by its extensive commentary and woodcuts. Daniele Barbaro’s Venetian edition of 1556, with contributions by Palladio, belongs to a later stage of that reception. Petrarch’s engagement with Vitruvius was Latin and scholarly; it should not be confused with these printed vernacular translations. 164
