Vitruvius and his Work John Ruskin's quotation, while methodologically brilliant in contrasting the 19th-century view with the classical one, introduces a dichotomy (architect vs. builder) that did not exist in that form in the Roman world: for Vitruvius, the architect is the ultimate builder because he masters both fabrica (manual practice) and ratiocinatio (mathematical theory). Furthermore, in the last paragraph, it is crucial to clarify that for Vitruvius, architecture does not imitate nature in its formal or ornamental aspects, but rather in its operational principles and rational laws (tectonic mimesis). “In the programmatic design of De architectura, Vitruvius (c. 80–15 BCE) configures the building discipline not as an empirical or sectoral craft, but as an encyclopedic and unifying episteme. By assigning it a primordial epistemic character, the treatise writer maintains that architecture subsumes and structures practically all areas of human knowledge. For Vitruvius, excellence in architectura demands a bidirectional training founded on the symbiosis of fabrica (executive practice) and ratiocinatio (the theoretical and mathematical demonstration of proportions). This universal propaedeutic requires of the architect a rigorous mastery of a broad spectrum of disciplines: • Geometry (Geometria): An indispensable instrumental axiom for the delineation of plans (ichnographia), elevations (orthographia) and perspectives (scaenographia), guaranteeing the exact translation of abstract diagrams into physical space. • Mathematics (Arithmetic): Foundation of modular metrology and cost calculation, essential for the computation of symmetries and proportionality relationships that ensure tectonic stability against material loads. • Anatomy and Medicine (Medicine): An analytical prescription that governs sacred anthropometry — synthesized in the canon of homo bene figuratus — and urban health. It includes the study of climatic vectors, water quality, and the sanitation of residential districts. • Optics and Acoustics (Optice et Musica): Physical knowledge applied to the correction of optical illusions in the entablatures and tonal 167

calibration of the theaters through the harmonic use of resonating vessels or echeia. • Law (Iura): Knowledge of Roman civil and urban planning jurisprudence, regulating easements of light, drainage, party walls and construction contracts to avoid tax disputes. • Theology and Astrology (Theologia et Astrologia): Doctrines that determine the correct observance of decorum (decor), ensuring that the typologies of the temples correspond to the ontological attributes of each deity, as well as for the layout of the solar quadrants (gnomonica) and the cosmic orientation of the oracular cellas. • Meteorology (Caeli Ratio): Microclimatic analysis of the geographical environment that determines the orientation of openings, the thickness of walls and ventilation systems according to the prevailing winds. The Historical Dialectic of Design and Tectonic Mimesis This holistic vision of the architect as a universal sage contrasts with the aestheticist derivations of modernity. Centuries later, the 19th-century critic John Ruskin would condense the Romantic turn by stating that “no one who is not a great sculptor or painter can be an architect; if he is not, he can only be a builder.” For Vitruvian pragmatism, however, beauty (venustas) is not a plastic ornament superimposed by the fine arts, but a mathematical property emerging from correct structural arrangement. In Vitruvian cosmology, architecture operates under the principle of mimicking nature, not through the slavish copying of its biomorphic forms, but through the emulation of its laws of efficiency and protection. Just as birds and bees configure their nests in response to instinctive needs for preservation, primitive humanity erected the primitive hut as a primary refuge against the harshness of the elements. The transition from this primitive organic functionalism to the refinement of the art of building was completed when Hellenic civilization translated the tectonics of wood into the laws of stone, canonizing this process through the invention of the architectural orders: the structural vigor of the Doric, the golden elegance of the Ionic, and the vegetal exuberance of the Corinthian. 168

PRELIMINARY STUDY Critical Notes 1. The Vitruvian-Ruskin Tension: It is excellent to introduce Ruskin. Ruskin writes from the perspective of Romanticism and the Gothic Revival, where the architect is an individual artist and the builder is a mere industrial worker. For Vitruvius, this separation is an aberration: the fabric (knowing how to lay the bricks) and the ratiocinatio (knowing why they are laid) form an indissoluble unity. By recovering this Roman sense, this edition advocates a return to the unity of thought and matter. 2. The Primitive Hut as Archetype: Vitruvius's account of the origins of architecture (Book II) is the foundation of all Western architectural theory (later revisited by Laugier in the 18th century). The hut of logs and leaves is the "womb" of architecture. The Greeks did not invent the orders from nothing; they petrified the wooden structure of the hut (the triglyphs of the Doric order are the stony memory of the original beam ends). Architecture is, therefore, an alchemical transmutation: converting the ephemeral wood of nature into the eternal order of geometric stone. 3. The concept of Decorum: In the theology section, it is essential to use the Vitruvian technical term Decorum. Decorum is the mystical suitability of the building to its function. Vitruvius explains that a temple to Minerva, Mars, or Hercules should be Doric (robust, austere, masculine), while a temple to Venus, Flora, or Proserpina should be Corinthian (delicate, slender, ornamental). The architectural order is not chosen for aesthetic taste, but for a cosmic correspondence with the energy of the divinity that will inhabit the space. " Vitruvian epistemology finds its operative core in the indissoluble symbiosis between fabrica and ratiocinatio. Vitruvius rigorously warns that those practitioners who devoted themselves exclusively to manual skill (fabrica) without the aid of letters failed to achieve an authority commensurate with their efforts; conversely, theorists who took refuge solely in abstract reasoning (ratiocinatio) pursued a shadow instead of material reality. Consequently, the architect of excellence is defined as that scholar capable of transmuting theory into practice, governing their activity by an encyclopedic knowledge that unifies the exact sciences, the liberal arts, and the humanistic culture of the imperium. " 169

This systematic approach unfolds with architectural rigor in the internal structure of De architectura, a corpus divided into ten books or volumes (volumina). Each section opens with a proemium (preface) of profound philosophical and historical depth that legitimizes the subsequent topic in light of the figure of Emperor Augustus. It is in Book I that the author establishes the three ontological and immutable vectors that must govern all construction, universally known as the Vitruvian triad: • Firmitas (Solidity): Guaranteed by the scientific selection of materials, the firmness of the foundations (substructio) and the correct distribution of structural loads without blindly relying on empirical resistance. • Utilitas (Utility or Functionality): Achieved through the functional and obstacle-free arrangement of the plants, ensuring that the distribution of spaces accurately reflects the public or private use for which they are intended. • Venustas (Beauty or Grace): An aesthetic emergence that is consolidated when the appearance of the plane is pleasing and harmonious, based on the laws of proportion (proportio) and the modular correspondence of the homo bene figuratus, whose geometric translation would inspire the Renaissance canon of Leonardo da Vinci. Dispositio Textus: Analytical Structure of the Ten Books The architecture of the Vitruvian treatise is structured according to the following thematic and philological ordering: Table 2. Analytical structure of the ten books (dispositio textus) Book Traditional Thematic Rubric Epistemological and Technical Content Book I On Architecture and the Planning of Encyclopedic training of the architect; the Cities theoretical triad; foundations of urban planning, castrametation and the defense of cities. Book II On the Properties of Materials Archaeology of the primitive hut and evolution of housing; physical-chemical study of building materials (sand, lime, pozzolana, brick and wood). Book III De sacrorum aedium symmetria Theory of body proportions and anthropometry (homo bene figuratus); typologies of the classical temple and symmetries of the Ionic order. 170

PRELIMINARY STUDY Book Traditional Thematic Rubric Epistemological and Technical Content Book IV De corinthio et dorico ordine Continuation of sacred treatises; genesis and laws of the Doric and Corinthian orders; proportions of altars and cellas. Book V De publicis locis Civil and institutional architecture of the forum; basilicas (with special attention to the Basilica of Fano); acoustics and geometry of theaters (echeia). Book VI De privatis aedificiis Domestic building; the Roman domus and the suburban villa; adaptation of housing according to social condition and climate. Book De expolitionibus Surface treatment; plastering techniques, VII stucco, paving and the chemistry of decorative pigments. Book De aqua Hydraulic engineering; prospecting, VIII collection, leveling and distribution of water; construction of aqueducts and cisterns. Book IX De gnomonica Applied cosmos sciences; elementary astronomy, lunar phases, meridian plotting and construction of sundials and water clocks. Book X Of machines Mechanics and polyorcethics; kinematic lifting devices, pneumatic hydraulics and manufacture of torsion artillery (ballistae). Through this rigorous compartmentalization of knowledge, De architectura consolidates itself as a living organism where each book acts as a modular block. The work demonstrates that the act of designing a simple brick (Book II) or calibrating a siege ballista (Book X) participates in the same mathematical matrix and the same rational order that governs the movement of the stars in the firmament (Book IX), configuring a true cosmology of construction. Critical Notes 1. The Interdependence of the Triad: It is crucial to emphasize that firmitas, utilitas, and venustas are neither optional nor divisible. In the Roman mindset, beauty (venustas) is not a superficial aesthetic added at the end; it is the direct result of the building being solid (firmitas) and perfectly fulfilling its function (utilitas). The proportion that makes a temple beautiful is the same mathematical proportion that prevents its dome or entablature from collapsing. 2. The Descending Order of Knowledge: The geometric beauty of the treatise's structure. Vitruvius begins in Book I by examining the entire territory 171

(the macrocosm of the city) and ends in Book X by analyzing the tooth of a gear or the rope of a catapult (the microcosm of the machine). There is a conscious descent from the divine laws of heaven and temples (Books III and IV) to the humble matter of the earth and military technology (Books VII and X). 3. The Link of Book II to the Origin: The transition from Book I to Book II is pivotal to the treatise's argument concerning development. Vitruvius introduces the materials (sand, stone, wood) immediately after explaining what a city is, because the raw material must be consecrated by the architect's logos before becoming a wall or temple. The clay of the earth is elevated to the category of classical order through the geometric intervention of the sage. • Book V (De publicis locis): Volume devoted to institutional architecture and the organization of civic meeting spaces. The author systematizes the proportions of the forum, the typology of the forum basilica (inserting his own construction experience in Fano) and, most importantly, the physics of theaters, where he introduces the science of harmonic acoustics and the optical optimization of the seating areas. • Book VI (De privatis aedificiis): Treatise dedicated to domestic architecture and the organization of private space. Vitruvius analyses the climatic orientation of rooms, the typologies of the atrium of the Roman domus, and the configuration of suburban villas, establishing that the dwelling should reflect the socioeconomic condition and the decorous status of its owner. • Book VII (De expolitionibus): A technical monograph focused on the arts of finishing and coating materials. It describes with engineering precision the preparation of mortar, the execution of high-strength pavements, the plastering of stuccos, and the mineral and vegetable chemistry for obtaining imperishable decorative pigments. • Book VIII (De aquis): Section dedicated to hydraulic engineering (aquarum ductus). Vitruvius addresses the geological prospecting of springs, the medicinal properties of waters, the methods of topographic leveling using the chorobates, and the technologies of conduction through masonry channels, lead pipes (fistulae), or clay (tubuli). • Book IX (On Gnomonics): A cosmological and physical -mathematical digression that links architecture with the celestial order. The author explains the foundations of geocentric astronomy, the movement of the 172

PRELIMINARY STUDY stars, and the geometry of analemmatic projections indispensable for the design of sundials (horology) and mechanical water clocks. The Paradox of the Lost Figures and the Hermeneutics of Space In terms of textual transmission, the definitive loss of the original graphic apparatus that complemented Vitruvius's manuscript constitutes one of the most influential phenomena in the history of Western architectural theory. Throughout his ten books, the author explicitly refers to diagrams and illustrations (figurae) —originally placed at the end of the papyrus scrolls — intended to visually clarify the complex geometric formulas of the orders, the eurhythmy of the facades, or the mechanisms of the lifting machines. The disappearance of this visual atlas during the early medieval manuscript copying process transformed De architectura into a purely abstract and conceptual text. However, far from diminishing its relevance, this absence of images became the main driving force behind European architectural thought. Lacking a single, unambiguous graphic model, architects and humanists — from Fra Giocondo and Cesare Cesariano to Andrea Palladio — were compelled to reinvent, draw, and design the treatise, forcing a dialectical confrontation between classical text and archaeological ruins. This hermeneutical gap transformed a rigid military manual from the Augustan era into a living, inexhaustible, and foundational text for the history of Western science and aesthetics. Critical Notes 1. The precision of Book VII: Maintaining pavements and plasterwork in Book VII. Vitruvius explains that a good plaster requires up to six layers of mortar made from lime and powdered marble. This is not merely decoration; it is the pursuit of material perfection. The wall should reflect light like a mirror. Venustas (beauty) is achieved when the craftsman's physical technique elevates opaque matter to a state of pure luminosity. 2. The Chorobates and the Leveling of the Land: In Book VIII, the use of the chorobates (a twenty-foot-long wooden ruler with plumb lines and a water channel for leveling) represents the imposition of the horizontal straight line upon the irregularity of the land. For water to flow to the city, the engineer must correct nature. Vitruvian hydraulics is, therefore, a branch of applied geometry that purifies and orders the land. 173

3. The Analemma of Book IX: The design of sundials using the analemma is mathematical proof that Roman architecture is a cosmological science. The architect projects onto the plane of the earth the shadows cast by the sun on its annual journey through the zodiac. A well-oriented Vitruvian building is not isolated from its surroundings; it is an astronomical instrument that beats in unison with the time of the universe. The space of architecture and the time of the stars are unified under the rule of the treatise writer. Translation (1847), published in Paris by Panckoucke, is one of the cornerstones of 19th-century French philology. Maufras's great merit was to strip Vitruvius's text of the overly romantic interpretations of his time, restoring the technical rigor and military pragmatism of the Latin original. In line with contemporary editorial standards, chapter titles are standardized by combining Maufras's 19th-century rubric with modern technical-legal and archaeological concepts (such as the distinction between publica and privata in urban land-use planning). STUDY OF THE TEN BOOKS Academic Restitution and Writing (Books I and II) The structural breakdown of the first two books of De architectura reveals the epistemic matrix upon which Vitruvius builds the entirety of his treatise. Far from constituting a mere summary of trades, the index of these foundational books traces the ontological transition that runs from the training of the scholar and the geopolitical delimitation of territory (Book I) to the physico-chemical analysis of raw materials and the anthropology of building (Book II). The systematic organization of these chapters is reconfigured under the following academic standard: BOOK I: De architectura et de urbis ordinatione (From architectural science and the organization of urban space) • Chapter I: The epistemology of building and the propaedeutics of the architect. Definition of the discipline through the coexistence of the fabric and the ratiocinatio; breakdown of the encyclopedic training of the professional. • Chapter II: The constitutive axioms of architecture. Analysis of the six theoretical principles that govern classical design: ordinatio (arrangement), dispositio (arrangement), eurythmia (eurhythmy), symmetria (symmetry), decor (decorum) and distributio (distribution or economy). 174

PRELIMINARY STUDY • Chapter III: The parts of architectural science and the ontological triad. Division of knowledge in the construction of buildings (aedificatio), gnomonic (gnomonice) and mechanics (machinatio). Introduction of the three universal requirements: firmitas, utilitas and venustas. • Chapter IV: Environmental Teratology and Selection of Urban Sites (De electione locorum sanissimorum). Hygienist and Hippocratic Criteria for the Founding of Cities; Analysis of Winds, Marsh Fogs, and the Salubrity of Humours. • Chapter V: Poliorcetics and Fortification: The erection of walls and towers. Deep foundation techniques (substructio) and defensive geometry to repel enemy siege engines. • Chapter VI: Climatic urbanism and street orientation. Street layout and interpolation of walls based on the wind rose (anemometry) to neutralize harmful currents in public space. • Chapter VII: Sacred and civil zoning (Dispositio moeniorum). Spatial distribution and allocation of plots for the temples of the immortal gods and the common spaces of the citizens according to liturgical decorum. BOOK II: De materiae facultatibus (From the physical and chemical properties of materials and the origin of tectonics) • Chapter I: Cultural Anthropology and the Genesis of Building. Account of the primitive hut; the domestication of fire as the origin of human society and the transition from the cave to the geometric order. • Chapter II: Cosmology of the elements according to the philosophical schools. Theory of matter based on the pre-Socratic principles (Thales' water, Anaximenes' air, Heraclitus ' fire and Democritus' atoms) as the key to understanding building materials. • Chapter III: The adobe brick (De lateribus). Modular typologies (Lydian, pentador, tetrador), seasonal drying processes and quality control of clay. • Chapter IV: Sand (From harena). Mineralogy classification of quarry sands (fossicia), river sands (flumina) and sea sands (marina), and their suitability for mortar cohesion. 175

• Chapter V: Lime (From calce). Chemistry of the calcination of limestone and the agglomeration of the stone components. • Chapter VI: Pozzolan (De pulvere puteolan). The discovery of volcanic dust from the regions of Baiae and Vesuvius; the technological miracle of hydraulic setting (mortar capable of solidifying underwater). Critical Notes 1. On the rendering of pulvere puteolanum: the Roman term pulvere puteolanum corresponds directly to modern pozzolana. This chapter (II.6) is among the most important in the history of Roman civil engineering: pozzolana allowed the Romans to build ports, docks, and bridge foundations submerged directly in water, breaking the limitation of Greek architecture, which always relied on dry rock. 2. Chapter VI of Book I as cosmic geometry: The layout of streets according to the winds was not merely a matter of convenience. Vitruvius describes the placement of a gnomon (a vertical pillar) in the center of the future city to mark the line of the shadow in the morning and afternoon. By joining these points, the East-West line was obtained, and from there the city was divided into a perfect octagon corresponding to the eight principal winds. The Roman city is, therefore, an inhabited sundial, a sacred space perfectly oriented with the axes of the cosmos. 3. From Atom to Brick: In the order of the chapters of Book II, Vitruvius does not jump directly to explaining how to build a wall; he first dedicates an entire chapter (Chapter II) to the philosophy of matter. He explains that to be a good architect, one must understand the behavior of the four elements of nature, because brick, lime, and wood expand, contract, and react according to the invisible laws of pre-Socratic physics. Knowledge always precedes technique.100 Books III and IV of De architectura constitute the dogmatic core of the theory of sacred design in Antiquity. Vitruvius articulates a system where beauty (venustas) is not a subjective criterion, but an emergent mathematical property based on the module (M). Book III takes the human microcosm as its starting 100Pozzolans are siliceous or aluminosiliceous materials of volcanic origin which, mixed with lime, set in the presence of water. They are fundamental to Roman opus caementicium. 176

PRELIMINARY STUDY point to dictate the laws of the Ionic order, while Book IV expands this grammar to encompass the vigor of the Doric and the slenderness of the Corinthian, establishing altar typologies according to liturgical decorum. The systematic organization of these chapters is established under the following academic standard: BOOK III: De sacrorum aedium symmetria (On the symmetries and proportions of sacred temples) • Proem: Apology for the merits of the architect in the face of the injustice of political favor; the immortality of classical treatise writers through the written word. • Chapter I: Anthropometry as the matrix of sacred design (homo bene figuratus). Study of the proportions of the human body and its exact inscription in the perfect figures of the circle and the square; derivation of the perfect numerical system (6, 10 and 16) from anatomy. • Chapter II: Typological classification of temples according to their facades. Geometric definition and distribution of the colonnade: temple in amphiprostyle, prostyle, in antis, dipterous, pseudodipterous and peripterous. • Chapter III: Classification of temples according to the intercolumniation (Modulatio). Analysis of the five types of temples based on the distance between columns measured in modules: pycnostylos (thick), systylos (narrow), diastylos (wide), araeostylos (dilated) and eustylos (ideal harmonic proportion). • Chapter IV: Stereobate and deep foundation (De fundamentalis). Excavation techniques and foundation engineering in firm soil or artificial ground using charred wooden piles; construction of the steps (stylobata) and the calculation of the odd scamilli to correct the optical illusions of subsidence on the horizontal line. • Chapter V: The Ionic Order: From the shaft to the entablature. Laws of proportion of the Ionic column: the layout of the base, the reduction of the shaft by means of the entasis (optical curvature), the geometric design of the volute of the capital, and the measurements of the architrave, the frieze and the cornice. BOOK IV: De corinthio et dorico ordine 177

(On the architectural orders and the arrangement of the cellas) • Proem: Justification of the continuity of Book III; the need to exhaust the study of the three architectural orders of Hellenic tradition before addressing civil spaces. • Chapter I: The Corinthian Order and the Mythological Genesis of its Proportions. Origin of the Corinthian capital through the anecdote of Callimachus in Corinth and the acanthus basket on the maiden's tomb; analysis of the slenderness of the order as an imitation of the graceful figure of a virgin. • Chapter II: Archaeology of wood and the petrification of the Doric order. Exegesis of tectonic mimesis; how the stone elements of the Doric order (triglyphs, metopes, mutules and drops) are the direct translation and memory of the beams, rafters and wooden joints of the primitive hut. • Chapter III: The metric laws of the Doric order and its design difficulties. The problem of the corner triglyph (Doric angular conflict); exact distribution of modules in the metopes, columns and entablatures to avoid spatial asymmetry. • Chapter IV: Internal arrangement of the temple: The cella and the pronaos. Geometric distribution of the interior walls, the proportions of the naves and the metric relationship between the space of the divinity and the exterior facade. • Chapter V: Cosmic Orientation of Sacred Architecture. Astrological and Liturgical Prescription: The cellas of the temples must be inexorably oriented towards the west, so that the faithful approaching the altar face the east, from where the sunlight originates. • Chapter VI: The doors and openings of the temples. Proportions and profiles of the openings according to three classical typologies: Doric, Ionic and Tuscan (Attic). • Chapter VII: The temples of the Tuscan order (De tuscanicis aedibus). Structural features and proportions of the temple of Italic or Etruscan tradition, characterized by its wide wooden eaves and its almost quadrangular plan. • Chapter VIII: Circular Temples and Altars of the Gods. Geometry of centrally planned temples (tholos) and round peripteral temples; rules for the erection of altars (arae) placed according to the celestial, terrestrial, or chthonic rank of the invoked deity. 178

PRELIMINARY STUDY Critical Notes 1. The Scamilli Impares as a Geometric Secret: In Book III, Chapter IV, Maufras translates the technical term scamilli impares as "unequal bearings." This is one of the most debated passages among Renaissance architects. It refers to the subtle upward curve given to the stylobate (the temple platform). If the platform were perfectly straight in the geometric plane, the human eye would perceive it as sunken due to an optical distortion. By curving it slightly towards the center, the temple appears perfectly stable and regular to the observer. True symmetry requires curving the material straight line. 2. The Doric Angular Conflict as a Mathematical Dilemma: Chapter III of Book IV explains why Greek architects (such as Tarcesius) abandoned the Doric order for the Ionic: due to the rigidity of the triglyph. By law, a triglyph must be positioned exactly over the center of each column and the center of each intercolumniation. However, at the corners of the temple, the triglyph must be placed at the very edge of the frieze, which misaligns the last metope. This dilemma forced the shift from a two-dimensional approach (the façade) to a three-dimensional adjustment of the intercolumniation (corner contraction). Classical geometry prefers to change the physical module rather than disrupt the visual harmony of the whole. 3. The Altar as a Cosmic Interface: The final chapter of Book IV eloquently concludes the hypothesis concerning Delphi and the archetypes. Vitruvius details that the altars of Jupiter and the celestial gods should be elevated; those of Gaia and the underworld (chthonic) deities should be rustic and at ground level; and those of the water nymphs should be intermediate. The altar is the vanishing point where the geometry of the temple communicates with the invisible forces of nature, the same principle that united the ashes of the serpent Python beneath the oracular omphalos of Delphi. From the interior of the cells and the distribution of the pronaos101. Regarding the orientation of the temples. Temple doors and door frames; their proportions 101Pronaos (πρόναος, from πρό, ‘before’, and ναός, ‘temple’) denotes the space in front of a temple’s naos or cella. It forms the temple’s vestibule or entrance and commonly continues the cella’s principal axis. The Latin forms are borrowings from Greek, not the source of the Greek word. 179

of the Tuscan order102. We now turn to the middle block of the corpus: Books V, VI, and VII. In these books the text makes the great leap from the rigidity of sacred architecture to the flexibility of Roman civil life and technological pragmatism. The transmission of the passage concerning the palaestra requires care: corrupt readings may obscure its reference to the covered porticoes called xysti (xystos). The title of Book VII, De vitiis, likewise denotes the defects and faults of construction, not any matter of conduct or instruction. “Books V, VI, and VII of De architectura depict the transition from the cosmic space of the gods to the anthropocentric stage of the Roman citizen. Book V regulates the monumentality of the civil fabric (theaters and ports); Book VI theorizes about domestic intimacy (the domus and the villa), adapting it to the climate and social status; and Book VII functions as a rigorous manual of applied chemistry, analyzing coating techniques and the nature of pigments.” The organization of these chapters under a contemporary critical standard is structured as follows: BOOK V: De publicis locis (Of civil architecture and monumental public spaces) • Proem: Justification of the brevity of technical books; defense of the plain and instructive style against the traditional literary rhetoric of philosophers. • Chapter I: The Roman Forum and the legal basilicas. Proportions of the forum in relation to gladiatorial spectacles; geometry of the judicial basilica and case study of the lost Forensic Basilica of Fano erected by Vitruvius himself. • Chapter II: State Logistics: The Treasury, the Prison and the Curia. Technical arrangement of the offices of the public treasury (aerarium), the state prisons and the town hall or municipal palace (curia), guaranteeing their visual harmony with the forum. 102The Tuscan arrangement described by Vitruvius at 4.7 derives from the Etrusco-Italic temple: a column with a simple base, an unfluted shaft and an undecorated capital, with robust proportions. Renaissance theorists, including Serlio, Vignola and Palladio, codified it as the first and simplest of the architectural orders. 180

PRELIMINARY STUDY • Chapter III: The Theater: Environmental Hygiene and Seating Geometry. Criteria for selecting the theater site; exclusion of unhealthy areas to protect the throat and breathing of spectators from harmful air currents. • Chapter IV: Science of music and canonical harmony. Mathematical digression based on the Pythagorean theories of Aristo Xeno; division of musical intervals (harmonic, chromatic and diatonic) essential for architectural acoustics. • Chapter V: The resonating vessels of the theater (Echeia). Symmetrical placement of bronze or clay vases in niches under the seats; tonal calibration in intervals of fourth, fifth and octave to mechanically amplify the human voice. • Chapter VI: Geometric layout of the Roman theater. Inscription of four equilateral triangles within a regular circle to determine the width of the stage (proscaenium), the pulpit (pulpitum) and the accesses of the orchestra. • Chapter VII: Design Variations: The Greek Traditional Theater. Metrical differences with the Roman model; expansion of the orchestra and reduction of the stage for the Hellenic chorus. • Chapter VIII: The roof and porticoes of the theater stage. Aerial acoustics of the stage; inclination of the upper roofs and their function as reflectors of sound waves. • Chapter IX: Public walkways and post-stage porticoes. Design of porticoes behind the theater (porticus post scaenam) as a refuge for citizens from sudden rain; planning of green areas and tree-lined walkways for their therapeutic and hygienic virtues. • Chapter X: The Baths: Hydraulics and thermodynamics of the Roman bath. Arrangement and solar orientation of the saunas and pools; construction technique of the hypocaust (hypocastum or radiant floor) and distribution of the caldarium, tepidarium and frigidarium. • Chapter XI: The Palaestra: Architecture of athletics and the Xysti. Organization of the training courtyards; design of the covered porticoes or xysti intended for physical exercise during the winter. • Chapter XII: Port engineering and submerged hydraulic structures. Construction of docks, dikes and breakwaters; use of wooden caissons (arcae) for water drainage and application of pozzolan hydraulic mortar for the solidification of concrete underwater. 181

BOOK VI: De privatis aedificiis (On domestic architecture and the organization of private buildings) • Proem: Praise of education and knowledge as the only wealth that survives the shipwreck; the dignity of the profession in the face of the speculation of upstart builders. • Chapter I: Architectural Climatology and Medical Geography. Suitability of dwellings according to the latitude of the imperium; thick walls and shady orientations for the southern provinces (Egypt), and wide openings oriented to the south for the cold northern regions (Gaul and Germania). • Chapter II: Eurythmy and optical corrections in residential scale. Modification of theoretical proportions based on the actual dimensions of the plot, ensuring that the eye perceives the rooms as balanced despite the constraints of the terrain. • Chapter III: Anatomy of the Domus: From the Atrium to the Peristyle. Modular typologies and measurements of the cavaedium or atrium (Tuscan, Corinthian, tetrastyle, displuviate and testudinate); dimensions of the wings (alae), the office of the pater familias (tablinum), the dining rooms (triclinia) and the reception rooms (exedrae). • Chapter IV: Heliothermal orientation of private rooms. Prescription for health and comfort: bedrooms and libraries should face east to take advantage of the morning light; winter dining rooms should face west to capture the heat of the sunset; and art galleries or painting galleries should face north to maintain a constant luminosity that does not degrade the colors. • Chapter V: Sociology of residential space. Distribution of housing in relation to the public rank of the inhabitant; need for majestic private vestibules and basilicas for magistrates and nobles who receive clients, versus modest houses for moneylenders or artisans. • Chapter VI: Rural Architecture: The Rustic Villa. Planning of farms and country houses; arrangement of stables, wine cellars, oil presses (torcularia) and barns according to ventilation and prevention of dampness. • Chapter VII: The Hellenic house and its differences with the Roman one. Structure of the Greek house; strict division between the gynaeceum (women's space) and the andronitis (men's hall); the porticoed courtyards, foreign to the Italic atrium system. 182

On the title of Book VII (De vitiis): the phrase denotes the material defects, hidden flaws, and faults in the execution of a work — not pedagogy or morality. Third Pictorial Style as Geometric Transgression: Chapter V of Book VII contains Vitruvius's famous moral complaint against the painters of 184

PRELIMINARY STUDY his time. Vitruvius hated the fantastic Pompeian style because it depicted thin reeds supporting heavy roofs, or human figures sprouting from flowers. For him, this was a violation of structural truth. If a reed cannot support a roof in material reality (firmitas), painting that reed supporting a roof on the wall is an aesthetic lie that destroys ratiocinatio. Decoration must be subordinate to the immutable laws of physics and statics. These two books demonstrate that Roman architecture was not confined to the earth’s surface: Book VIII descends into the depths of the crust through hydraulic engineering, while Book IX rises to the celestial vault through analemmatic and gnomonic astronomy. It is essential to clarify that Vitruvius’s astronomical digression is not an ornamental addition, but the necessary mathematical basis enabling the architect to measure time (sundials) and to orient buildings with respect to the solstices and equinoxes. " Books VIII and IX of De architectura represent the expansion of the discipline of building to encompass the two great fluids of the cosmos: subterranean water and celestial light. Book VIII functions as a treatise on applied geology and fluid engineering, systematizing everything from hidden prospecting to the construction of cisterns; meanwhile, Book IX operates as a compendium of geocentric astrophysics, dictating the mechanical laws that allow the capture of the sun's shadow to regulate the time of civilization." Contemporary analytical standard is broken down as follows: BOOK VIII: De aqua hydraulic engineering and water prospecting) • Proem: Praise of water as the primordial element of the cosmos; its absolute necessity for the survival of life and ritual purity in the face of the other elements of nature. • Chapter I: Geological prospecting and detection of hidden sources (De inventione aquae). Techniques of observing the terrain at dawn; analysis of indicator vegetation (rushes, willows, ivies) and methods of test excavation using inverted bronze vessels to capture the condensation of telluric vapor. • Chapter II: The hydrological cycle and rainwater. The fundamental mathematical method for projecting the three-dimensional curve of the sun's path onto a two-dimensional flat surface using a ruler and compass, serving as a matrix for any latitude on Earth. • Chapter VIII: Gnomonics: Typologies of sundials and water clocks. Catalog of inventors and models of sundials (horologia): the hemicycle of Berossus, the scaphe of Aristarchus, the plinth of Scopinas, and description of the complex mechanisms of clepsydras or automatic water clocks driven by gears and regulated floats (inventions of Ctesibius). Critical Notes 1. Opus Signinum and Roman hydraulic waterproofing: In Chapter VII of Book VIII, Vitruvius treats lime and cement cisterns. Philologically, the Roman term is opus signinum (lime mortar mixed with fragments of pottery and crushed tiles). The addition of the pottery triggers a chemical reaction that renders the mortar absolutely impermeable. This detail is technically significant: the channeled water is retained without seepage within a watertight lining of opus signinum. 187

2. The analemma of Book IX: geometric projection in gnomonics: Chapter VII of Book IX is a scientific core for the study of regulated space. The analemma is not an artistic drawing; it is a pure geometric construction that projects the apparent annual motion of the Sun, mapping it onto the twodimensional plane of the dial. By mastering the analemma, the Roman architect could calculate the exact shadow a building would cast at any time of day and on any day of the year (equinoxes and solstices). The method thus allowed the architect to represent, on a plane surface, the geometry governing the Sun's apparent course throughout the year. 3. The Inverted Siphon (Venter) and the Mastery of Gravity: In Book VIII, Chapter VII, the description of the lead pipes crossing the valleys demonstrates that Roman engineers understood the physics of communicating vessels. To prevent water pressure from breaking the pipes at the bottom of the valley, they constructed a horizontal section called a venter (belly). Roman engineering did not evade the forces of gravity, but rather balanced them through the symmetry of the watercourse. Astronomy is used to predict changes in the weather, and what will happen to men, based on the appearance of the stars at the time of their birth. How to make an analemma103. Since the invention of summer clocks or sundials; Clepsydras and winter or anaphoric clocks.104 105 103In Vitruvius (9.1.1; 9.7), the analemma (ἀνάλημμα) is a geometrical projection used to lay out a sundial’s hour lines. It is distinct from the figure-of-eight curve also called an analemma in modern astronomy. 104 A clepsydra (from the Greek κλεψύδρα, kléptein,"To steal, and ὕδωρ hydōr," water") is any mechanism for measuring time by the regulated flow of a liquid into or out of a graduated container, thus giving rise to two different types of clocks depending on the direction of the flow. Clepsydras date back to ancient Egypt (mrḫyt) and were used especially at night, when sundials were no longer useful. The earliest water clocks consisted of a ceramic vessel filled with water to a certain level, with a hole at the base of a suitable size to ensure the liquid flowed out at a specific rate and, therefore, in a predetermined time. The container had several markings inside, so that the water level indicated the different periods, both day and night. 105Ctesibius (Κτησίβιος), active in third-century BCE Alexandria, was an inventor and hydraulic and mechanical engineer. PRELIMINARY STUDY This final book distils Vitruvius’s pragmatism in its purest form — that of a legionary military engineer. One technical term calls for care: the Latin cochlea must be rendered as the Archimedes’ screw (the water-screw, or auger pump for raising fluids), not by any popular nineteenth-century equivalent. We also systematise the direct influence of this book on the seminal treatises of antiquity and the Renaissance. Book X of De architectura crowns the work not as a technical appendix, but as the dynamic manifestation of physics and geometry applied to the service of the Roman state. Vitruvius breaks down the laws of elementary kinematics, distinguishing between large traction machines and precision devices, before turning to industrial hydraulics and military torsion ballistics, whose mathematical calibration depended directly on the geometric solution of doubling the cube. The organization of these chapters is reconfigured under the following contemporary critical standard: BOOK X: De machinis (From mechanical science, fluid engineering, and poliorcetics) • Proem: Ethical and economic considerations on the budgets of public works; the severe laws of the city of Ephesus that forced architects to answer with their own assets in case of financial deviations, and an apology for prudence in the administration of the State's resources. • Chapter I: Epistemology of mechanics and definition of machine. Conceptual distinction between the machine (machina), which requires the participation of several operators and displays high mechanical performance, and the instrument or organ (organum), operated by the skill of a single individual. • Chapter II: Kinematic lifting and traction devices. Description and breakdown of the loading cranes (trispastos, pentaspastos and polyspastos) used in temple construction; calculation of pulleys, winches, capstans and the physics of levers. • Chapter III: Kinematic Theory: The Straight Line and Circular Motion. Analysis of the physical principles of motion; how the combination of rectilinear and circular forces governs the operation of all machines, exemplified in ship rudders and scales. 189

• Chapter IV: Hydraulic lifting engineering: Drums and waterwheels. Mechanisms designed to extract water from rivers and shallow wells by means of paddle wheels and compartmentalized drums powered by human traction (tympana). • Chapter V: Watermills and industrial waterwheels. The automation of milling; description of the Roman angle gear that transmits the movement from the vertical shaft of the waterwheel to the horizontal shaft of the millstones for grinding the grain. • Chapter VI: The Archimedes’ screw (cochlea). Analysis of the waterscrew: the geometric design of the helix wrapped about a wooden cylinder to raise large volumes of water through a low lift, as used in draining mines and fields. • Chapter VII: Ctesibius's impeller pump. Pneumatics and precision engineering; description of the double - cylinder bronze machine provided with pistons, valves and suction pipes capable of raising water to great heights for fire extinguishing. • Chapter VIII: The Hydraulic Organ (Hydraulus). The pinnacle of ancient mechanical precision; application of the laws of hydraulic pneumatics to regulate air pressure by means of water, making flutes and pipes sound through a mechanical keyboard. • Chapter IX: Odometry: Measurement of distances on land and sea. Description of the mechanical odometer or classical taximeter; a system of reducing gears coupled to the wheels of a cart (or to the paddles of a ship) that dropped small bronze spheres into a container for each mile traveled. • Chapter X: Military Torsion Ballistics: Catapults and Scorpions. Principles of Poliorcetics; Calculation of the diameter of the torsion cord module (made of tendons or human hair) based on the weight of the projectile or arrow that the scorpion was to fire. • Chapter XI: Engineering of the Ballista (Ballistae). Mathematical proportions and calibration tables for the construction of large pieces of artillery intended for launching heavy stones to demolish walls. • Chapter XII: Calibration and tempering of torsion cords. Methodology for symmetrically tensioning the arms of catapults and ballistae using acoustic nut wrenches, ensuring that both torsion modules vibrate with the same musical note to guarantee a straight trajectory for the shot. 190

PRELIMINARY STUDY Vitruvian Tradition and the Family Tree of Architectural Theory The disappearance of the original figures (estimated at a minimum of ten modular plates affixed to the ends of the papyrus scrolls by Vitruvius himself) forced 16th-century editors to undertake a colossal graphic reconstruction. This hermeneutical effort gave rise to the creation of the great modern treatises, which adopted the Vitruvian theoretical framework and adapted it to the needs of their respective eras. • Pliny the Elder (Natural History, 1st century AD): An immediate contemporary in the historiographical record. Pliny absorbed and indexed Vitruvius's mineralogical and metallurgical investigations (particularly the data in Book VII on cinnabar, lime, and marbles) within his books dedicated to geology and the plastic arts, validating the soundness of science during the time of Augustus. • Leon Battista Alberti (De re aedificatoria, 1452): The first great treatise of Renaissance humanism. Alberti adopts the decemviral structure (ten books) and cardinal concepts of Vitruvius, but purifies the medievalized technical Latin of the Roman under the lens of Ciceronian prose and Platonic philosophy, transforming the Vitruvian triad into the supreme concept of Concinnitas. • Andrea Palladio (I quattro libri dell'architettura, 1570): The apotheosis of visual codification. Palladio synthesizes Vitruvius's abstract theory and translates it into a practical system illustrated with engravings of perfect geometric symmetry. Through his four books, Palladio applies the module and proportions of Vitruvian temples (Books III and IV) to the design of urban palaces and residential villas, universalizing the classical canon in Western architecture. Critical Notes 1. The cochlea (Archimedes’ screw): the Latin cochlea designates the water-screw and must be rendered accordingly, not by any popular nineteenthcentury term. It effects the transformation of continuous circular motion into an upward linear flow of fluid — one of the great achievements of applied helical geometry, showing that the Roman architect had mastered the principles of hydraulics. 191

2. Music as a regulator of warfare: Chapter XII of Book X. Vitruvius details how military engineers had to tune the catapult strings by musical ear. If one arm of the ballista was tighter than the other, the projectile would be deflected. This demonstrates that the harmonic music of Book V (designed for theaters) and the physics of warfare in Book X share the same mathematical framework. Music is not an art of entertainment; it is the physical law that balances both the voice in the sacred space and destructive energy on the battlefield. 3. Odometry as the Metric of the Empire: The invention of the odometer (Chapter IX) is the materialization of the control of Roman space. By inventing a machine that mechanically counts miles, architecture aligns itself with Agrippa's cartography: the untamed territory of the barbarian provinces is fragmented, measured, and dominated by the geometric regularity of the odometer. Measured space is space conquered by Ratio. De architectura, Marcus Vitruvius Pollio; c. 80 – 70 BCE – d. after 15 BCE), probably written around 15 BCE The chronology agreed upon by modern philologists (such as Pierre Gros and Louis Callebat) places the birth of Marcus Vitruvius Pollio around 80–70 BCE and his death around 15 BCE. His magnum opus, De architectura, was written progressively and dedicated to Octavian Augustus between 27 BCE and 23 BCE (coinciding with the consolidation of the Principate and the great urban renewal program of Rome), although some technical appendices could be revised until 15 BCE. " The treatise De architectura, the only theoretical corpus of Greco-Roman architecture preserved in its entirety, was composed by the engineer and military architect Marcus Vitruvius Pollio (c. 80/70 BCE – 15 BCE). The internal chronology of the text places its main phase of writing between 27 BCE and 23 BCE, a critical period in the history of the West marked by the transition from the Roman Republic to the Principate of Octavian Augustus." Vitruvius conceived his ten books not as a descriptive manual a posteriori, but as a programmatic and legitimizing manifesto of the new political order. By dedicating the work to the Imperator, the author aligned geometric science and construction techniques with the official program of the Restitutio Reipublicae. The treatise served as the conceptual framework for the 192

PRELIMINARY STUDY monumentalization of public space, providing Augustus with the architectural tools necessary to fulfill his celebrated historiographical maxim: to have received a Rome built of brick (latericia) and to bequeath to posterity a metropolis clad in marble (marmorea). The dating of the work, fixed in its definitive edition around 15 BCE, closes the era of Hellenistic influence on the Italian peninsula and inaugurates the construction canon of the global Empire. Critical Notes 1. The significance of 27 BCE: In this year, Octavian received the sacred title of Augustus from the Senate. This is the precise moment when Vitruvius decided to present him with the treatise. This is not a chronological coincidence: Vitruvius knew that a new Empire needed a new architecture that reflected stability, order, and eternity (firmitas). It should be emphasized that the ten books constitute the geometric constitution of Augustus's Empire. 2. The Pax Romana as a technical requirement: Vitruvius confesses in the Proem of Book I that, while the Roman state was mired in civil wars (against Julius Caesar, Mark Antony, and Pompey), he dedicated himself to artillery and legionary ballistics. Only when Augustus pacified the world (Pax Romana) could the architect withdraw the siege engines and devote himself to theorizing about temples and forums. The order of sacred space was only possible when the chaos of war ceased. 3. The transition from the papyrus scroll (volumina) to the modern book: around 15 BCE, Vitruvius presented Augustus with ten separate papyrus scrolls (volumina). The concept of a single bound book is a late antique and medieval development. This physical separation explains why each book has its own independent preface (proemium): each scroll was opened and read before the emperor as a separate discursive and scientific unit. Editing Criteria and Translation Note The Latin passages in this edition are checked against Fritz Krohn’s Vitruvii de architectura libri decem (Leipzig: B. G. Teubner, 1912). Rose (1899), the Budé volumes and modern translations provide further points of comparison where specifically cited. This procedure must be distinguished from a new collation of the manuscripts: a reading attributed to a manuscript requires an identifiable 193

witness and a verifiable source in a critical apparatus or a documented inspection of the relevant folio. Morgan’s The Ten Books on Architecture (1914) and the translation by Ingrid D. Rowland, with commentary and illustrations by Thomas Noble Howe (1999), provide two important twentieth-century points of comparison. Their interpretations are consulted where relevant to a technical or historical problem; neither replaces the author’s Spanish translation as the source of the English. A reference to these works should not be taken as certification that every passage has been newly collated against them. This work has a prologue of a humanistic nature by Eugenio Montes, member of the Royal Spanish Academy, and presents a careful vernacular translation made by the philologist and professor of the Complutense University, Carmen Andreu. Technical revision, which was entrusted to Dr. Fernando Higueras, an architect who was then in charge of the real estate division of the aforementioned company. Higueras's intervention in Vitruvius's text represents a milestone of considerable interest for contemporary architectural theory: a master of structural organicism and expressive structuralism of the 1970s reinterpreting the geometric rigor of the 1st century BC. This edition not only functioned as a collector's item, but also as a hermeneutical bridge where classical prescriptions regarding the hygienic environment, materials, and modular symmetry were reread through the lens of the 20th-century architectural avant-garde. Methodological notes 1. Krohn’s contribution (1912). His Teubner edition offers an important critical constitution of Vitruvius’s text and an apparatus that distinguishes transmitted readings from editorial interventions. It should be consulted alongside Rose and the relevant Budé volume. No edition restores an unmediated “pure” manuscript text: readings must be assessed at individual 194

and European rationalism, periods marked by two publishing ventures of universal significance: • Claude Perrault's rationalist recension (1673/1684): Published under the title Les dix livres d'architecture de Vitruve, corrigez et traduits en françois, the work of the physician, scientist, and architect Claude Perrault transformed the foundations of the discipline. Perrault applied the Cartesian method and the rigor of the Académie des Sciences to the Latin text. His fundamental contribution lay in the demystification of the mystical character of classical proportions; the French scholar argued that beauty (venustas) did not respond to divine or immutable laws of nature, but to a cultural and arbitrary pact of architects (the invention of taste). His sumptuous array of engravings not only illustrated the elusive lost figures, but also served to legitimize the design of the Louvre colonnade, establishing the canon of French Classicism. • The pinnacle of the Hispanic Enlightenment: José Ortiz y Sanz (1787): Following the partial attempts of the preceding century, the priest and Enlightenment thinker Joseph Ortiz y Sanz completed the monumental translation: The Ten Books of Architectura by Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, translated from the Latin and annotated. Printed in Madrid by the prestigious Royal Printing House in an imposing folio format of 42.5 cm, this work marked Spain's entry into modern architectural philology. Ortiz y Sanz did not limit himself to translating; he collated the Vatican codices by hand, corrected the errors accumulated by the Italian translators, and endowed the volume of 56 copperplate engravings with millimeter - level archaeological precision. Sponsored directly by the Bourbon reforms of Charles III and Charles IV, this edition served as the obligatory reference text for the Royal Academy of Fine Arts of San Fernando, eradicating the decorative excesses of the late Baroque and establishing the rigor of Neoclassicism on Iberian soil. PRELIMINARY STUDY Vitruvius Pollio, M. The Ten Books of Architecture by Marcus Vitruvius, 1787. Pollion (J. Ortiz y Sanz, Trans. and Com.). Madrid: Royal Printing Press. (In-folio, XXVIII, 277 pp., LVI plates). Exegetical notes 1. Claude Perrault's theoretical fracture: this point is crucial for assessing the persistence of a sacred geometry or cosmic order. Perrault opens a wound in the history of architecture: he argues that the golden ratio and the homo bene figuratus are not divine truths. For Perrault, the eyes become accustomed to seeing buildings in a certain way, and that is why they seem beautiful to us, not because they reflect the order of heaven (Book IX). Perrault thus marks the shift from architecture as mysticism and cosmology to architecture as an engineering science and cultural convention. 2. The Royal Printing Press and the Political Control of Order: The Ortiz y Sanz edition (1787) was not a literary whim. The enlightened Spanish state needed to standardize architecture to control its territory (just as Augustus did in 15 BCE). By decreeing that all churches, town halls, and hospitals in the Spanish Empire (including Spanish America) had to follow the 56 plates of Ortiz y Sanz, the Crown used Vitruvian principles to visually standardize the urban landscape and bury the Churrigueresque style. Geometry once again became an instrument of political sovereignty and the ordering of matter. 3. The value of the 56 plates by Ortiz and Sanz: Unlike the Renaissance illustrations of Cesare Cesariano or Palladio (who adapted Vitruvius to their own architectural tastes), the plates by Ortiz and Sanz are characterized by obsessive philological rigor. The Spanish Enlightenment thinker measured ancient monuments, striving to understand the precise mathematics of the texts without adding Baroque or modern embellishments. They represent the birth of modern archaeological technical drawing in the Hispanic world. Regarding the name of the treatise: For the palaeographical and philological assessment, particular attention must be given to Harley MS 2767 (H), held by the British Library. The manuscript, 197

copied in Caroline minuscule in the first quarter of the ninth century, is the oldest known surviving witness to Vitruvius’s De architectura. The British Library catalogs Cologne or Aachen as possible places of origin, and an association with Charlemagne’s palace scriptorium remains conjectural. Medieval manuscripts identify works through opening and closing formulas, conventionally called incipit and explicit, as well as through rubrics. These forms belong to the history of transmission and must be distinguished from the title pages of printed editions. The British Library’s catalogue records the opening of Harley MS 2767 as follows: 1. The opening formula The cataloged text begins with the title of Book I and the dedication to Caesar. The catalogue gives the incipit as: “Vitruvii de Architectura liber I. Cum divina tua mens et numen, Imperator Caesar.” This report attests the medieval transmission of the title De architectura. Its capitalization and punctuation here follow the catalogue rather than a fresh diplomatic transcription of the folio. The closing formula and the ten-book structure The British Library records De architectura on ff. 1r–162v, followed by a recipe added after the explicit. The ten-book structure is also established internally by Vitruvius’s prefaces and cross-references. Book X ends with accounts of siege defense, rather than a chapter devoted solely to torsion engines. For the witness’s contents and physical description, see the British Library catalogue, Harley MS 2767. The incipit and explicit are documentary formulas whose precise spelling should be cited from the relevant folio or from an explicitly identified catalogue report. PRAEFATIO EDITORIS Lectori docto, salutem. Opus Marci Vitruvii Pollionis, De architectura, quod non modo antiquae constructionis rationes, sed etiam universam artium liberalium disciplinam complectitur, diu sub umbra translationum vitiosarum delituit. In hac editione nostra, quae anno bis millesimo vicesimo sexto in lucem profertur, propositum nostrum fuit textum ex editionibus criticis receptum diligenter exponere, lectiones incertas indicare et rationes architectonicas studiosis explanare. Non ignoramus, in hoc vetusto opere, multos locos ob linguam technicam, quae Graecis vocabulis abundat, difficiles esse intellectu. At vero, cum machinae nostrae aetatis echeia pro echo vel chorobaten pro saltatore vertissent, philologiae officium erat verum sensum mechanicum et geometricum restituere. Non est enim vitruvianus textus ad voluptatem legentis scriptus, sed ad aedificandum et ad machinas movendas; unde oportet verba eius tamquam instrumenta ipsa — sicut perpendiculum, regulam, aut circinum — percipi. In apparatu critico, qui in fine voluminis stat, rationem reddimus emendationum nostrarum, errores quosdam anachronismosque, qui in editionibus vulgaribus pervulgati sunt, aperte demonstrantes. Speramus igitur hanc nostram operam — Sophia Lux Publishing auspice edita — non modo architectis et ingeniariis, sed etiam philologis et historiae cultoribus, tamquam firmum fundamentum ad opus vitruvianum intellegendum inservituram esse. PRELIMINARY STUDY Praefatio editoris · Editorial principles This section sets out, for the benefit of the scholarly reader, the nature of the present edition, the text that underlies it, the scope of its critical apparatus, and the orthographic and translational conventions adopted throughout. Nature and base text This is a bilingual reading edition with a selective critical apparatus. The authorial Spanish translation by Diego Kurilo is the source of the English translation. Its Latin base is Fritz Krohn’s edition (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), checked against Valentin Rose (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899); the Budé volumes provide further critical and architectural reference by book. A printed or electronic edition is distinguished from a direct reading of an individual manuscript. Where the text departs from the adopted edition, or where a reading remains disputed, the difference must be identified in the apparatus. Scope of the apparatus The critical apparatus of this edition is selective and illustrative rather than exhaustive. It does not record every variant of every witness lemma by lemma, as the great systematic editions (Teubner, Budé) do; instead it concentrates on the passages of decisive importance for the constitution, the dating or the interpretation of the text, which are treated in the Apparatus criticus (Appendix M) and in the analytical restitution of the Greek vocabulary (Appendix N). The reader who requires a full positive apparatus is referred to the editions of Rose, Krohn and the Collection Budé. This limitation is stated openly so that the edition may be judged for what it is: a critical reading edition addressed to the architect and the historian of architecture, uniting the philological apparatus with the technical and architectural analysis. Orthographic conventions In the running Latin text the consonantal u/v is normalized in the modern manner (utilitas, Vitruvius), the classical majuscule V being retained only in display titles and rubrics that reproduce the epigraphic and manuscript usage (DE ARCHITECTVRA). The diphthong ae is written in full; consonantal i is not distinguished as j. Greek words are given in their restored polytonic form, 201

with the correct breathings and accents, accompanied where useful by a Latin transliteration; the principles of restitution are set out in Appendix N. Translation The English translation derives from Diego Kurilo’s original Spanish translation, itself made directly from Latin. Its governing aim is fidelity to that authorial interpretation, with Latin used to check doubtful technical terms, concepts and numbers. Granger and Rowland–Howe are comparative references rather than replacement source translations. Technical terms without exact modern equivalents—firmitas, utilitas, venustas, symmetria, ordinatio and dispositio—are retained in Latin where necessary and defined in the Glossary (Appendix A). 202

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I The meaning of the Text (Academic Analysis) In this first paragraph of the preface, Vitruvius uses an extremely elaborate Latin period (a typical construction of rhetorical prose) to address Augustus with great reverence. The fundamental meaning is as follows: Vitruvius justifies the delay in publishing his work De architectura. He explains that, while Augustus was at the height of his power — having pacified the Roman world after the civil wars — he did not dare to distract him with his writings on architecture. The author uses language laden with courtly flattery (typical of Augustan literature): • He describes Augustus's mind as divine and mentions his numen (divine force). • His undefeated military virtus stands out. • It presents the emperor as absolute ruler of the world (imperio potiretur orbis terrarum). • He describes how the Roman people and the Senate, freed from fear, are guided by Augustus’s judgment. With this rich rhetoric, Vitruvius achieves two objectives: 1. Demonstrate humility and respect before the princeps. 2. Carefully choosing the moment to dedicate his work: precisely when Augustus has achieved universal peace and can dedicate himself to cultural and construction projects. This introduction sets the tone for the entire treatise: a technical work presented under imperial protection and seeking to contribute to Augustus's program of architectural and cultural renewal. M. · LIBER I cornices on top of them, he will give the following explanation to those who ask him: The city of Caryae, in the Peloponnese, allied itself with the Persians, enemies of Greece. Subsequently, the Greeks, gloriously liberated by their victory in the war, declared war on the inhabitants of Caryae by common agreement. Therefore, having captured the city, killed the men, and razed the city, they led its matrons into servitude, not allowing them to remove their tunics or matronly ornaments, so that they would not be paraded only once in triumph, but rather, oppressed by grave affront and as an eternal example of servitude, they would seem to atone before posterity for the guilt of their city. For this reason, the architects of that time depicted their images in public buildings carrying a burden, so that the memory of the punishment for the crime of the women of Caryae would also reach future generations. Explanation of the Meaning of the Text This paragraph is one of Vitruvius' most famous and constitutes the legendary origin of the caryatids. Key points: 1. The Usefulness of History: The architect must not only know how to build, but also provide cultural and historical justification for the ornamental elements he employs. For Vitruvius, architecture is an eloquent art that “speaks” through its forms. 2. The caryatid narrative: Vitruvius gives an aetiological explanation for the architectural figure. He names Caryae in the Peloponnese, which must be distinguished from Caria in Asia Minor. His account presents the loadbearing women as an enduring image of the punishment and humiliation imposed on their city. The historical status of that account remains distinct from its symbolic function in the treatise. 3. Symbolic value: This passage illustrates how Roman (and Greek) architecture used figurative elements with a strong moral and commemorative content. M. Vitruvii Pollionis scholarship associates instead with archaic korai and the cult of Artemis Caryatis, whose ritual dances were performed by the girls of Caryae. 225

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I Academic translation “Philosophy, for its part, perfects the architect in spirit, so that he is not arrogant, but rather gentle, fair, and loyal, and — most importantly — free from avarice. For no work can truly be accomplished without loyalty and integrity. Let him not be covetous or preoccupied with receiving gifts, but let him uphold his dignity with gravity, maintaining a good reputation. And this is precisely what philosophy prescribes.” Furthermore, philosophy explains the nature of things, what in Greek is called physiologia, a body of knowledge that must be mastered with special dedication, since it encompasses many and varied natural matters, as is also the case with water management. Indeed, the impulses, circulations, and pressures of natural air occur in very different ways depending on the differences in elevation and forced conduits; and no one will be able to solve their problems without knowing, thanks to philosophy, the principles of nature. Likewise, whoever reads the precepts written by Ctesibius, Archimedes, and other authors of the same kind will not be able to fully understand them unless they have been instructed in these matters by philosophers. Explanation of the Meaning of the Text In this paragraph, Vitruvius explains the fundamental role of philosophy in the training of the architect, dividing it into two main aspects: 1. Moral (ethical) formation: Philosophy shapes the architect's character, instilling essential virtues such as humility, fairness, fidelity, and above all, the absence of greed. Vitruvius emphasizes that moral integrity (fides et castitas) is indispensable for practising the profession with dignity. 2. Scientific training (physics / physiology): Architects need knowledge of natural philosophy to understand complex physical phenomena, especially in hydraulics (aqueducts, water and air pressure). Without these principles, they would be unable to solve real-world technical problems. Vitruvius further links theory with practice by mentioning great Hellenistic engineers (Ctesibius and Archimedes), whose treatises can only be properly understood with a philosophical basis. This passage reinforces the Vitruvian ideal of the architect as a complete professional: not just a technician, but a cultured, ethical and scientifically trained man. 230

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I Academic translation “Likewise, he must know music, in order to master canonical reason and mathematical notation, and to be able to correctly adjust the tensions of the ballistas, catapults and scorpions.” Indeed, in the capitals of these machines there are, on the right and left, holes for the hemitonia, through which twisted cords of sinew are tensioned by means of capstans and levers. These cords are not locked or permanently fixed until they produce, to the ear of the craftsman, an equal and uniform sound on both sides. For the arms that are inserted into these tensions, when extended, must deliver the blow equally and evenly. If they are not in the same pitch (homotonic), they will prevent the projectiles from being launched straight. Explanation of the Meaning of the Text (Academic Analysis) In this paragraph, Vitruvius justifies the need for the architect to master music (understood as harmonic and acoustic theory) for an eminently practical reason: the calibration of torsion war machines. Key points: 1. Connection between music and mechanics: Vitruvius establishes a direct relationship between musical theory (harmonic proportions, tones, intervals) and military engineering. The correct tension of the machine's strings is achieved by ear, applying acoustic principles (sonitus certos et aequales). 2. Key technical concept: Homoton (equal pitch/equal tension). If the two halves of the torsion engine are not perfectly balanced, the weapon will lose accuracy and the projectile will deviate from its trajectory. 3. vision of architecture: This example perfectly illustrates the Vitruvian thesis: the architect is not only a builder, but a technician -scientist who must apply knowledge from different disciplines (in this case, music) to concrete problems of design and execution. This passage is especially interesting because it shows how, in Antiquity, disciplines that we now consider separate (music and military art) were closely linked through mathematics and the theory of proportions. M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I those who have brought a single field to the highest distinction through their own diligence and practice. This, however, cannot be achieved in reality.”112 Critical and Hermeneutic Translation “12. Those unfamiliar with the subject (inperitis) may find it surprising that human nature can master and retain so many disciplines. Once they recognize the close connection and mutual exchange among all branches of knowledge, however, they will readily believe it possible. Encyclopedic education (encyclios disciplina) forms a single body composed of these members. Those trained in different fields from an early age therefore recognize the same features and the connections shared by all the disciplines, and so understand everything more readily. For this reason Pytheos, the distinguished architect of Minerva’s temple at Priene, states in his commentaries that an architect should be able to accomplish more in every art and discipline than specialists who, through sustained practice, have brought a single field to the highest distinction.” However, the latter is not feasible in reality. Exegetical Notes 1. The Encyclios Disciplina as a mystical body: Vitruvius uses a metaphor of Stoic and Platonic origin: education is a living organism (uti corpus unum), where geometry, music, and astronomy are not isolated sciences, but rather the "members" (membris) of a single being. This is fundamental: the architect does not accumulate knowledge in a fragmented way; the architect understands the common mathematical root that unites sound (music) with space (geometry) and time (astronomy). 2. The rectification of Pytheus (The tension between Idea and Matter): Pytheus (the great Hellenistic architect of the Temple of Priene and the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus) was a radical in his theory; he asserted that the architect should know more about painting than a painter and more about sculpture than a sculptor. Vitruvius, with the Roman pragmatism that characterizes his framework, reins him in by closing the paragraph: Id autem re non expeditur. Vitruvius knows that human beings have physical limitations. 112Encyclios disciplina concerns an interconnected general education. The expression is related to Greek ἐγκύκλιος παιδεία (enkyklios paideia); it is distinct from the later ecclesiastical use of “encyclical”. 240
