VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I medicine (aniatrologetos); finally, he is not required to excel in the other sciences, but he must have a knowledge of them that is not inexperienced (non inperitus).” In the midst of such a vast variety of subjects, no one can achieve singular mastery or refinement (elegantias singulares), since knowing and thoroughly assimilating its theoretical principles (ratiocinationes) is something that barely falls within the capabilities of the human intellect. Exegetical notes 1. The constellation of Hellenistic archetypes: Vitruvius here maps out the greatest sages of the classical world to define the boundaries of architecture. He cites Aristarchus (the great grammarian of Alexandria who standardized Homer's text), Aristoxenus (the great theorist of music and the harmonic scale), Apelles (Alexander the Great's favorite painter), Myron and Polyclitus (the fathers of the canon of Greek sculpture), and Hippocrates (the father of medicine). By contrasting the architect with these giants, Vitruvius demonstrates that architecture is an integrative discipline: the architect does not displace the specialist, but rather acts as the conductor who coordinates all these areas of knowledge within the realm of the building. 2. The structure of double negations (non agrammatos, non amusos): This philological subtlety is relevant. Vitruvius does not use Vulgar Latin; he resorts to negated Hellenisms to indicate a state of critical competence. The architect does not have to compose a symphony like Aristoxenus, but he cannot be amusos (deaf to harmony), because if he were, he would not know how to place the acoustic vessels in the theater (Book V). He does not have to sculpt the Doryphoros like Polyclitus, but he must understand ratio plastica so that the statues of the caryatids maintain the modular proportion with the entablature. It is an apologia for the knowledge of synthesis. 3. The Limit of Human Power: The paragraph's conclusion is a lesson in epistemological humility in the face of Pytheus’s abstract intellectualism. Vitruvius acknowledges that the absolute mastery of the singular refinements (elegantias singulares) of each science eludes the power (potestas) of human understanding. Architecture, therefore, is defined as the science of the possible and the harmonious: it prioritizes the balance of the whole over the hyper- 242

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I Critical and Hermeneutic Translation “14. And yet, not only are architects unable to achieve supreme perfection (summum effectum) in all matters, but even those who possess exclusive mastery of a particular art (privatim proprietates tenent artium) do not, in their entirety, attain the highest principality of glory. Therefore, if in individual sciences particular artists — and of them not all, but only a few throughout the ages (aevo perpetuo) —have barely achieved renown, how is it possible that an architect, who must be skilled in multiple arts, accomplishes the prodigious and admirable feat not only of lacking none of the necessary knowledge in them (ne quid ex is indigeat), but of surpassing even all those artisans and specialists who have devoted absolute assiduity and the utmost industry to a single doctrine? ” Exegetical notes 1. Deconstructing the Myth of the Absolute Sage: This passage is a compelling argument for disassociating Vitruvius from the hyperbolic readings of the Renaissance. While the humanists of the Quattrocento sought to find in this chapter the justification for the absolute "universal man" (the unattainable polymath), Vitruvius's actual text is a lesson in Roman pragmatism and legal moderation. Vitruvius argues that the architect's goal is elemental selfsufficiency: "ne quid ex is indigeat " (that nothing should be foreign or lacking to him). The architect should not be a rival to the painter or the musician, but a valid interlocutor who understands the codes of each craft. 2. Specialized diligence versus spatial synthesis: Vitruvius contrasts adsiduitas (the specialist's obsessive and constant dedication to a single thing) with the architect's panoramic vision. The genius of architectural design lies not in fragmentary execution, but in symphonic coordination. The specialist works on the detail; the architect works on the relationship between the details. This distinction is fundamental to your theoretical framework, as it positions architecture as a second-order science or meta-discipline, whose object of study is not isolated matter, but the order that unifies the parts. 3. The Status of Nobility in the Arts: The use of the terms nobilitatem and laudis principatum reflects the Augustan mindset regarding the social status of the intellectual and the artisan. Vitruvius is attempting to elevate the profession of architecture above purely manual (fabrica) or servile labor. By demonstrating that the architect operates with the theory of all the arts, he 244

VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I principles of each discipline that are necessary for architecture, so that he is not found wanting when required to judge and approve matters concerning them.” Critical and Hermeneutic Translation “16. Similarly, there exists a common sphere of debate (disputatio communis) between astrologers and musicians regarding the cosmic sympathy of the stars and musical consonances, structured according to the relationships of squares and trigons, and the intervals of fourth (diatessaron) and fifth (diapente); likewise, the architect shares with geometers the science of vision, which in Greek is called λόγος ὀπτικός (logos optikos or perspective). In short, in all branches of knowledge, many subjects — if not all — are common to scholars exclusively on the level of theoretical argumentation (ad disputandum).” On the contrary, the practical execution of works (operum vero ingressus), which are brought to perfection and elegance by the hands and the skilled manipulation, belongs exclusively to those who have been properly trained and instructed in a single manual craft. Consequently, it is to be considered that an architect who possesses a moderate knowledge (mediocriter) of the principles and parts of each science—those strictly necessary for architecture—is more than adequately fulfilling (satis abunde) his duty, so that if it were necessary to issue a technical judgment or approve a project governed by these arts, his authority would not be deficient (ne deficiat). Exegetical notes 1. Astrology and Cosmic Aspects: This passage constitutes one of the most fascinating pieces of documentary evidence of Roman architectural Pythagoreanism. Vitruvius equates the musical intervals of a fourth (diatessaron, ratio 4:3) and a fifth (diapente, ratio 3:2) with the geometric configurations traced by the stars in the firmament when they form squares (square aspect, 90 °) and trines (trine aspect, 120 °). This fact confirms that Vitruvian architectural space is a resonant microcosm: temples and theaters are designed imitating the same metric proportions with which God tensions the strings of the heavens and the planets. 2. Logos optikos and architectural perception. The Greek expression λόγος ὀπτικός provides an important conceptual context for the optical adjustments discussed in Books III and IV. Greek geometric perspective taught that the human eye distorts the material line (making it 248

They left to posterity many mechanical and gnomonic inventions discovered and explained through calculation and the principles of nature.” Critical Translation and Hermeneutics “17. On the contrary, those beings whom nature has endowed with such skill (sollertiae), keenness of mind, and memory that they are capable of assimilating geometry, astronomy, music, and the other liberal arts in a profound and absolute way (penitus), surpass the limits and duties proper to architects (officia architectorum) to become pure mathematicians. For this reason, it is extremely easy for them to debate and challenge any of these disciplines, since they are equipped with the vastest arsenal of theoretical projectiles (pluribus telis disciplinarum). However, such men appear exceptionally in history, as Aristarchus of Samos, Philolaus and Archytas of Tarentum, Apollonius of Perga, Eratosthenes of Cyrene, Archimedes, and Scopinas of Syracuse once were; colossi who bequeathed to posterity a vast quantity of mechanical devices (res organicas) and gnomonic instruments (gnomonicas), discovered and rigorously explained through numerical calculation and the physical laws of nature (numero naturalibusque rationibus). 114 Philolaus, also known as Philolaus of Tarentum or of Croton (Greek Φιλόλαος, Philolaos; c. 470–c. 380 BC), was a Greek Pythagorean and Presocratic philosopher, mathematician, astronomer, politician, music theorist and writer. He held that all matter consists of limiting and unlimited things joined by harmony, and that the universe is determined by numbers. He is credited with originating the hypothesis that the Earth was not the center of the universe, a theory included in the Pythagorean astronomical system. 115 Archytas of Tarentum (Greek Ἀρχύτας ὁ Ταραντίνος; c. 430–c. 360 BC) was a philosopher, mathematician, astronomer, statesman, general and contemporary of Plato. He worked in his native city, the Greek colony of Tarentum in Apulia, and belonged to the Pythagorean tradition. 116 Apollonius of Perga, also called Perge (Greek Ἀπολλώνιος; c. 262 BC–Alexandria, c. 190 BC), was a Greek mathematician and astronomer renowned for his work on conic sections. He gave the names ellipse, parabola and hyperbola to the curves now known by those terms. His study of conic sections informed later geometrical problem-solving; it should not be equated uncritically with the symbolic solution of general

· LIBER I Exegetical Notes 1. The ontological distinction: Architect versus Mathematician: Vitruvius defines the boundaries of the profession in relation to pure science. The architect needs theory to order physical matter, but his ultimate goal is the building, the structure. The mathematician, on the other hand, operates on a purely intellectual plane; he transcends the need to build because his mind masters the abstract laws that govern the universe. By placing mathematicians above the architect, Vitruvius demonstrates brilliant epistemological honesty: architecture is not the queen of the sciences because it is the most abstract, but because it synthesizes abstract thought for the benefit of civilization. 2. The pantheon of Hellenistic polymaths: The names cited constitute the canon of the Hellenistic scientific revolution analyzed here: ◦ Aristarchus of Samos: The first to propose the heliocentric model of the universe. ◦ Philolaus and Archytas of Tarentum: Pythagorean philosophers; Archytas was the father of mathematical mechanics and a friend of Plato. ◦ Apollonius of Perga: The geometer who revolutionized the study of conic sections (ellipse, parabola and hyperbola). ◦ Eratosthenes of Cyrene: The sage who calculated the circumference of the Earth with astonishing accuracy by measuring the shadows at the solstice. ◦ Archimedes of Syracuse: The greatest mechanical and hydrostatic genius of antiquity, inventor of the burning mirrors and the claws that defended Syracuse. ◦ Scopinas of Syracuse: Famous inventor of complex sundials and linear gnomonic mechanisms. 3. The Duality of the Organic and the Gnonomic: Vitruvius closes the chapter by connecting this ending with the books that complete his treatise: the machines of Book X (res organicas) and the clocks of Book IX (gnomonicas). By pointing out that these inventions were explained by numero naturalibusque rationibus, Vitruvius offers us the interpretive key to his treatise: the machine and the clock are not products of chance or blind craftsmanship; they are the material crystallization of the mathematical laws of nature. The mathematician discovers them in the heavens, and the architect applies them on Earth. 251

· LIBER I Likewise, aedificantibus means “those engaged in building”, not “edifiers” in a moral sense. Critical and Hermeneutic Translation “18. Therefore, since the possession of such intellectual gifts and natural ingenuity is not granted indiscriminately to all nations but to a small number of exceptional men, and since the architect's craft must be practised within the full range of liberal arts, the very nature of the discipline — due to its colossal scope (propter amplitudinem rei) —allows for the possession not necessarily of the highest degree in these sciences, but rather a moderate knowledge (mediocres scientias) of them. For this reason, I beg you, Caesar, both you and all those who will read these volumes (volumina sunt lecturi), to forgive me if any passage has been explained in a manner that does not conform to the rules of grammatical composition.” I have endeavored to write these pages not in the style of an eminent philosopher, nor of an eloquent rhetorician, nor of a grammarian trained in the subtlest rules of his art, but rigorously like an architect steeped in literature. Nevertheless, with regard to the intrinsic power of the profession (artis potestate) and the rational principles that are integrated within it (ratiocinationes), I firmly commit myself — or so I hope — to offering in these volumes an unquestionable authority (maxima auctoritate), useful not only to builders (aedificantibus), but also to all scholars. Exegetical notes 1. The material form of reading. Roman volumina were commonly papyrus rolls rather than bound codices. This historical context helps explain the material act of reading, but the adopted wording is volumina sunt lecturi, “those who will read these volumes”. It neither prescribes a particular movement of the hands nor supports an emendation to levaturi. 2. The legitimization of technical prose: Vitruvius here constructs a manifesto in favor of specialized technical language. By contrasting his style with that of the summus philosophus or the rhetor disertus, the author argues that architecture possesses its own syntax. The beauty of his text does not lie in the ornamentation of words (political or literary rhetoric), but in the precision with which the words reflect the ratiocinatio of the building. It is a defense of scientific literature: the architect writes as he builds, with solidity (firmitas) and structural clarity, renouncing the artifices of sophistical eloquence. 253

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I 3. The universal scope of the treatise (Omnibus sapientibus): The closing paragraph is the argument that unifies the thesis on Sophia. Vitruvius proudly proclaims that his work is not a mere catalog of constructions for masons or laborers (non modo aedificantibus). By including the sapientibus (the wise, the philosophers, the intellectual elite of the Empire), the treatise claims its place in the high culture of the Pax Romana. Vitruvius demonstrates that architecture is a knowledge of the State, a branch of applied philosophy indispensable for the ordering of the civilized world. The emperor governs men, the philosopher governs souls, and the architect builds the material space where both exercise their power. 254

· LIBER I proportions of the whole with symmetry (symmetria). This is composed of quantity (quantitas), which in Greek is called ποσότης (posótes). Quantity, in turn, is the adoption of modules (modulorum sumptio) from the members of the work themselves, as well as the harmonious and convenient effect of the whole of the building derived from each of the parts of said members.” Arrangement (dispositio), for its part, is the appropriate placement of elements and the elegant effect of the work resulting from their combinations according to their quality. The forms or categories of arrangement, which in Greek are called ἰδέαι (idéai), are these three: ichnography (ichnographia or plan), orthography (orthographia or elevation), and scaenographia (perspective). • Ichnography (the ground plan) is the disciplined and continuous use of rule and compass, by which the outlines of the forms are set out upon the ground plane. • The orthography is the vertical representation of the facade and a figure drawn to scale in a moderate way, reflecting the proportions of the future work. • Scaenographia, the perspectival representation is the sketch of the facade and the sides that recede into the distance, with all vanishing lines converging towards the center of a circle. These categories arise from meditation (cogitation) and invention (invention). Meditation is attentive reflection, full of assiduity, industry, and vigilance, which pursues the effect of the devised purpose with intellectual delight. Invention, on the other hand, is the resolution of obscure problems and the discovery of a new constructive principle through agile and vigorous ingenuity. These are the delimitations of the dispositions. Exegetical Notes 1. Quantitas as the Birth of the Module: Vitruvius defines quantitas (ποσότης) not as an absolute metric dimension (meters or fixed feet), but as a relative and modular dimension (modulorum sumptio). The architect takes a part of the building — for example, the diameter of the column — and that part becomes the module M. All the rest of the temple (height, width of the forum, intercolumniations) will be a multiple or submultiple of that module. Ordering is the abstract order that reduces the complexity of matter to a single generating number. 259

· LIBER I Just as the human body possesses the eurhythmic quality of symmetry, derived from the forearm, the foot, the palm, the finger, and other smaller parts, the same is true for the perfect execution of buildings. This is evident, first and foremost, in sacred temples, calculated either from the diameter or thickness of the columns (columnarum crassitudinibus), or from the triglyph (triglypho), or from the module (embater); similarly, it is found in military ballistics, derived from the diameter of the torsion opening in the capital (e foramine capituli), which the Greeks call περίτρητον (perítreton); and in ships, from the space between the oars, or interscalmus, called διάπηγμα (diapegma). Similarly, the analytical principle of symmetries (symmetriarum ratiocinatio) is discovered in any other type of work by examining its own members. Comparative critical apparatus — I.2.4. Embatere is adopted and the supplement <capituli> is made visible in ballista e foramine <capituli>, as in Krohn’s printed text (1912, 10, lines 18–20). The Greek terms require particular care: περίτρητον denotes the machine’s torsion opening. For the naval module associated with interscalmium, the Spanish edition’s running text has διάπηγμα, whereas its comparative note gives διπηχυια. Krohn’s printed text gives διπηχυαια and Rose (1899, 11, line 17) gives διάπηγμα. the authorial Spanish edition’s running reading is retained here, and the disagreement within the Spanish source is recorded rather than silently harmonized; the current Perseus transcription must not be assumed to reproduce every detail of Krohn’s Greek. Conceptual note — Symmetria. Here symmetria means commensurability or the modular correspondence of parts to a whole, rather than bilateral symmetry. The variety of examples—temple, ballista and ship—shows that Vitruvius formulates a principle of relative dimensioning applicable to different technical fields, rather than a single universal proportion. Exegetical Notes 1. Ancient symmetry does not mean the same as modern symmetry (a mirror image with respect to an axis). For Vitruvius, symmetry is the conveniens consensus (shared mathematical harmony). It is the proportional relationship that unites the parts with the whole. Its operational key is the rata pars (the aliquot or fixed part), which acts as the common metric divisor of the entire project. If the module (rata pars) measures 50 cm, the columns will measure 10×50 cm, the pediment 6×50 cm, and the forum 40×50 cm. 263

Exegetical Notes 1. Hygienic Urbanism and Medical Theology: Vitruvius demonstrates that Roman sacred architecture is neither capricious nor purely aesthetic; it is subject to the biological laws of nature. Placing a sanctuary (fanum) dedicated to healing deities like Asclepius or Salus in an unhealthy swamp would destroy the god's credibility. If the sick person recovers thanks to the pure air and clean water of the place (ex natura loci), they will miraculously attribute their cure to divine intervention, increasing the dignity and political prestige of the state religion. Architecture here acts as a strategic ally of preventive medicine. 2. Bioclimatic Architecture and Solar Orientation: This paragraph constitutes the first manual of thermal orientation in Western history. Vitruvius distributes the program of needs of the domus following the movement of the sun and the needs of the mind and body: ◦ East: For bedrooms and libraries. The morning light prevents dampness in books and awakens the intellect early. ◦ Winter West (Southwest): For winter bathrooms and lounges (hibernaculis). By opening towards the west, these rooms capture the heat accumulated throughout the afternoon, warming the space precisely during the hours when they will be used during the cold months. 3. However, Vitruvius performs a radical demythologization of the ritual: • Absence of the sacred: Livers are not examined to look for signs of the gods (such as caputiocineris or prophetic lines), but to check their objective physiological state (integram et solidam naturam). • Livestock as a bioindicator: Vitruvius understood that animals grazing in a fixed location act as a biological laboratory that metabolizes and concentrates the properties of the soil, the pastures (pabulum), and the water (aqua). If the liver shows necrosis or discoloration (livida et vitiosa), the ecosystem is corrupted. • The preliminary scientific method: The author describes a twostep verification protocol. If the first liver is damaged, more cattle are sacrificed (alia immolabant) to rule out an isolated pathology of the specimen (morbo) versus an endemic environmental poisoning (pabuli vitio). 3. The Theory of Miasma Contamination and Human Ecology The passage demonstrates the connection between Roman architecture and the medical theories of the Hippocratic school, specifically the treatise On Airs, Waters, and Places. Vitruvius establishes a direct correlation between animal and human health: the territory that destroys the organs of livestock will, sooner or later, destroy the constitution of the urban inhabitant (item humanis corporibus pestilentem futuram). The conclusion of the passage introduces a criterion for urban planning subordinated to ecology: if the environment is unhealthy, the solution is not constructive, but migratory (transmigrabant et mutabant regiones). Architecture cannot defeat nature; it must ally itself with its thermal and hydrological cycles. 4. Military Application: Castra Stativa The explicit mention of castra stativa (permanent camps or winter quarters) underscores the strategic importance of hygiene in Roman engineering. The Roman army could not afford epidemiological outbreaks in the legions stationed on the frontiers (limes). Analysis of the terrain using haruspicy (wisdom for livestock) was a mandatory step before the deployment of fixed defenses (munitiones), thus equating the rigor of military architecture with that of the founding of large civilian cities (oppida). 299

By ritually expelling the power of destructive fire (Volcani vi) from the high-density construction of the timber and masonry neighborhoods, the city was protected from catastrophic fires (timore incendiorum). ◦ Mars: The god of war must reside in the Campus Martius, the outdoor military training ground. Keeping the worship of weapons outside the domestic walls psychologically avoided internal violence, civil war, or coups d'état (armigera dissensio), projecting martial aggression exclusively towards the foreign enemy (ab hostibus ea defensa). 1.7.1 Once the road network was delimited, Vitruvius established the zoning of public plots (areae), combining commercial functionality with the Etruscan sacred tradition. While the forum was located at the port or the city center according to its geography, the Capitoline Triad (Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva) had to crown the highest point of the terrain for purposes of representation and surveillance. The sanctuaries of Mercury, Apollo, and Hercules were integrated into their respective economic and leisure districts. Conversely, following the writings of the haruspices, the temples of Venus, Vulcan, and Mars were segregated outside the city walls; This territorial planning policy sought to safeguard public morality, avert the danger of urban fires, and channel military force exclusively towards external defense against the enemy (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.7.1). 3. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II ARGUMENTUM LIBRI II — On the origin of architecture and civil life, and on building materials: brick, sand, lime, pozzolana, quarry stone, wall patterns (reticulatum, incertum, isódomon, pseudisódomon, émplecton) and woods, with their virtues and defects according to the proportion of natural elements. Notice. — Book II turns from theory to matter. After an anthropological preface on the origins of building — the primitive hut, society born around fire — it treats the materials of construction: brick, sand, lime, the volcanic pozzolana that sets under water, stone and quarries, the methods of walling (opus reticulatum, incertum, the Greek emplekton) and timber. It is the foundational ancient source for Roman building technology, and modern materials science has confirmed much of its account of lime and pozzolanic mortar. The passage of the human body inscribed in the circle and the square (3.1.3) is the root of a long modern interpretive tradition, with which this edition engages without uncritical adherence. Rudolf Wittkower (Architectural Principles in the Age of Humanism, 1949) read in Vitruvius the foundation of the humanist system of harmonic proportions binding man, building, and universe. Joseph Rykwert (The Dancing Column, 1996) explored the anthropomorphic root of the orders and the 'bodily' meaning of the column. Alberto Pérez-Gómez (Architecture and the Crisis of Modern Science, 1983) showed that Vitruvian sciographia is not modern linear perspective but a perception of the building's totality in depth. Indra Kagis McEwen (Vitruvius: Writing the Body of Architecture, 2003) set the treatise within the political-religious framework of Augustus and the body-architecture analogy. And Pierre Gros, editor of the Budé, has established the textual criticism and Vitruvius's relation to the tradition of the Greek treatises. This edition takes these contributions as its framework, distinguishes the datum of the text from its symbolic reading, and marks as 'the author's personal hermeneutic proposal' whatever exceeds what the text asserts. ARGUMENTUM LIBRI VI — On the private house: the influence of climate and latitude on the arrangement of buildings, the proportions of atriums, tablinums, peristyles and triclinia, the differences between the Greek and Roman house, and the suitability (decor) of each room to its use and the condition of its owner. Notice. — Book VI treats the private house. After a preface on the worth of learning above fortune, it relates domestic architecture to climate and latitude, sets out the proportions of the atrium, tablinum, peristyle and the several oeci, distinguishes the Greek house from the Roman, and turns to the working farmstead (villa rustica). These aims are properly achieved when the architect accepts advice from craftsmen and laypeople alike. ARGUMENTUM LIBRI VII — On finishes: the preparation of pavements and stuccos, lime plasters, ceiling moldings; natural and artificial colors and pigments (ochre, vermilion, purple, verdigris, ceruse) and their correct application. Notice. — Book VII, after a learned preface on plagiarism and the history of writing on architecture, treats the finishing of buildings: pavements and their bedding, the preparation of stucco and the technique of fresco, and the pigments — the natural earths and the manufactured colors, among them the synthetic Egyptian blue (caeruleum) and the lead and copper pigments. It is the most important ancient source on the technique of painting and the chemistry of pigments. Critical and structural note — VI.8. Vitruvius Today The Continuing Life of a Canon De architectura remains an active point of reference in architectural culture. Its contemporary value lies in the questions it brings together: how a building stands, how it serves its users, how its parts form an intelligible whole, and how the architect acquires the knowledge needed to judge these relationships. Three lines of reception connect that ancient inquiry with present practice. The triad of firmitas, utilitas and venustas continues to offer a concise framework for discussing durability, use and beauty. In the twentieth century, Le Corbusier’s Modulor developed a modern system of measure around the human body. It can be studied as a reinterpretation of the anthropometric tradition, while its aims and proportional rules remain distinct from those of Vitruvius. Symmetria, understood as the commensurability of the parts and the whole through a module, also invites comparison with design governed by relationships and rules. Parametric modeling makes such relationships explicit; Building Information Modeling coordinates information about design, construction and maintenance. These are contemporary analogies proposed by the author. They do not establish a direct technical descent from the ancient treatise. The discussions of site, orientation, healthy air, materials and water in Books I, VI and VIII likewise remain useful interlocutors for environmental design. Ancient explanations must be assessed within their own scientific and social setting. Reading firmitas today as durability and responsible use of resources extends the historical concept to a modern ethical concern; it does not attribute a present-day environmental agenda to Vitruvius. His continuing relevance is therefore best tested through informed comparison. The architect can learn from the relation between practical experience and reasoned explanation while examining the limits of both the ancient evidence and its later interpretations. That critical dialogue preserves the vitality of the canon without turning it into a timeless rulebook. 928

Janus and dactylonomy: a hermeneutic reading In the heart of the Forum Boarium, the Temple of Janus housed a statuary whose gestural configuration transcended mere ornamentation. The deity's hands were positioned according to the system of dactylonomy, configured to represent the number 355 (the duration of the Roman lunar year), symbolically adapting to the 365 - day cycle after the Julian reform. This codification was not accidental: it symbolized Janus's absolute dominion over time and his nature as absolute initium. This capacity of the hand to articulate complex theological concepts through coded gestures was a central component of Greco-Roman religiosity. A key testimony to this communicative power is found in Apuleius's The Golden Ass. In the description of the procession of Isis, the author recounts how a priest, carrying the sacred attributes, addresses the crowd and performs a specific gesture that was not a simple blessing, but a visual representation of secret knowledge — an initiatory teaching inaccessible to the uninitiated — 940

This edition stems from an extended study of the symbols, archetypes, and technical traditions linked to architecture and the art of building in classical antiquity. Through the figure of Marcus Vitruvius Pollio and his treatise De architectura, an attempt has been made to offer a comprehensive approach that combines historical and philological analysis with a hermeneutical reading of the symbolic dimensions present in the Greco -Roman architectural tradition. Vitruvius is not only the only architectural theorist whose complete works have survived from antiquity, but he also embodies a comprehensive conception of technical knowledge in which *fabricatio* and *ratiocinatio * — practice and theoretical reflection — are inextricably linked. His treatise, structured in ten books, constitutes a true encyclopedic corpus that reflects both the technical knowledge of his time and a vision of the architect as an intellectual versed in the liberal arts. The influence of De architectura far transcends its value as a construction manual. Its rediscovery and dissemination from the 15th century onwards decisively contributed to shaping the architectural thought of the Renaissance and the Modern Age. From Leon Battista Alberti to Andrea Palladio and Le Corbusier, by way of Leonardo da Vinci, the Vitruvian tradition has served as a guiding thread linking Antiquity with modernity. I arranged its distribution so that whoever is looking for a specific topic does not have to search for it in different parts, but rather has in each of the volumes a complete explanation of the different styles or genres, all in a single set. Vitruvius mentions that in Greece the number six was considered the emblem of physical nature and the generator of the cosmos. In this chapter, he recovers the Chaldean tradition which, since antiquity, attributed to the number six the representation of creation, considering it a perfect number. The Chaldeans classified their deities according to the number six, assigning the number 6 to minor gods and to wise men or teachers. The principal god, Anu, was represented by the number 60. Vitruvius mentions in his Book V that Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans wrote their theories and rules in volumes of cubic structure, called "cubicis rationibus", representing the cube as a set of 216 verses, where each rule did not exceed three verses. In the prologue to Book V, Vitruvius explicitly refers to the "cubic ratio " and the number 216 as a structural support of Pythagorean knowledge. This Vitruvian passage has been cited and commented on by various scholars as an example of the penetration of Pythagoreanism into Roman architectural culture during the Augustan period. See Rowland and Howe (1999), 66–67, for a discussion of the passage. Regarding the theoretical training of the architect, Vitruvius advocated education in the liberal arts. In doing so, he transferred the need, 951

expressed by Cicero, for a complete education for orators (rhetoric) to his own sphere, going back to the ancient Greek tradition of a comprehensive education (ἐγκύκλιος παιδεία, "enkykliospaideia"). This concept is reflected in his work through the term " encyclios disciplina [encyclopedic education; cf. Vitruvius, De architectura 1.1.12]". Vitruvius identifies ten areas of knowledge that an architect must master for the benefit of his architectural work: 1. Writing, 2. Drawing, 3. Geometry, 4. Arithmetic, 5. History, 6. Philosophy, 7. Music, 8. Medicine, 9. Law, 10. Astronomy. In his work, he addresses, among other topics, the dogmas of Plato and Pythagoras, and explains how Archimedes discovered the principle that bears his name, as well as the results obtained by Eratosthenes and Archytas of Tarentum when measuring the Earth. The highest temple of architecture Vitruvius prioritizes the ideal architect over the art of architecture, thus restricting access to the realm of architecture. The architect embodies architecture (a royal compendium of all things, united through art), but is only perfected through a comprehensive training course in various disciplines, which Vitruvius likens to a corpus. This discipline, the encyclios, 170has evoked the liberal arts for many readers, who imagine that Vitruvius invokes these disciplines to "elevate" architecture or even Vitruvius himself. However, it is also evident that architecture was already perceived as intellectually meticulous. By establishing a symmetry between his training (multidisciplinary but moderate) and his influence (which extends even to the products of all the other arts), Vitruvius creates a divide that evokes a similar disparity characteristic of the ideal orator in Cicero 's "De Oratore." Vitruvius recreates the ebb and flow of "De Oratore" to place architecture in competition with oratory as the supreme type of civic knowledge. Vitruvius’s account of human proportion in 3.1.2–3 may be summarized as follows: 953

1. Commensurability as a governing principle Vitruvius relates the proportional organization of a temple to that of a wellformed human body. The analogy concerns the commensurable relation of parts to the whole, rather than bilateral symmetry alone. He gives the following ratios: • The face: The face, from the chin to the top of the forehead (where the hair grows), should measure one - tenth of the man's total height. • The hand: The length of the hand, from the wrist to the tip of the middle finger, is also equal to one - tenth of the total height. • The head: From the chin to the crown, it represents one-eighth of the total height. • The upper chest: The distance from the upper chest to the hairline is one-sixth of the body’s height; the distance from the upper chest to the crown is one-quarter. 2. The circle and the square Vitruvius postulates that the human body has two inscribed geometric forms that demonstrate its proportional perfection: • The square: If a man stands with his arms extended horizontally, the distance between his fingertips (his wingspan) is equal to his total height. Thus, inscribing the body in a square results in a figure with equal sides. • The circle: If a man lies on his back with his legs and arms outstretched, his navel is the center point of his body. If a circle is drawn by placing a compass on his navel, the circumference will touch the tips of his fingers and toes. 3. The body as a unit of measurement (The module) Vitruvius insists that the measurements of the human body should be the basis for establishing "modules" in architecture: • The foot: It is equivalent to one sixth of the total height of a man. • The cubit (distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger): Represents one-quarter of the height. 4. Optica, defs. 1–4: the theory of visual rays, the mathematical basis for the optical corrections of columns (entasis) and for conical perspective (scaenographia) in Vitruvius III.4 and I.2. Hero of Alexandria, Mechanica / Pneumatica (Note: although Hero’s surviving work dates from the 1st c. AD, it reflects the Alexandrian science that Vitruvius assimilated in the 1st c. BC.) Mechanica I.1–5: the kinematic theory of gears, pulleys and compound tackle for lifting great weights, identical to the devices described in Vitruvius X.2. Pneumatica I.42: the description of the water-organ (hydraulus), corresponding almost point for point to the complex technical passage of Vitruvius X.8. Ptolemy, Analemma (Note: a testimony to the maturity of the sciences that Vitruvius sketches in their early phase.) Analemma 1–3: the geometric method of projecting the celestial sphere onto a plane for the design of sundials and quadrants, set out in rudimentary form in Vitruvius IX.1–7. 962

APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER APPENDIX I Testimonia veterum (Ancient Testimonies about Vitruvius) Antiquity and the early Middle Ages that mention Vitruvius or use his work are gathered. They constitute the documentary basis for reconstructing his biography and the fortune of De architectura, and explain why the treatise, far from being completely forgotten, enjoyed continuous transmission. Pliny the Elder, Natural History, indexes of books XVI and XXXV. He includes Vitruvius among the sources (auctores) he uses for the chapters on materials and pigments; it is the oldest testimony of the use of the work, barely one or two generations after its composition. Frontinus, De aquaeductu urbis Romae. The curator aquarum of Rome (c. 97 CE) agrees with Vitruvius in the measurements of the pipes (fistulae) and in the hydraulic doctrine, which proves the technical circulation of the treatise in the field of public administration. Faventino, De diversis fabricis architectonicae. Compendium from the 3rd-4th century AD that summarizes and transmits large portions of Vitruvius; It is the main late antique link in the tradition. Palladius, Opus agriculturae. He collects, through Faventinus, Vitruvian prescriptions on rural construction, disseminating them in medieval agronomic literature. Servius, Commentarii in Vergilii Aeneidem. The grammarian quotes Vitruvius on matters of architecture and religion, a sign of his authority in late antique teaching. Sidonius Apollinaris, Epistulae IV.3. He mentions Vitruvius as a model of technical knowledge, proof of his prestige in 5th century Gaul. Cassiodorus, Variae VII.5; Institutiones. He recommends the reading of Vitruvius to the officials in charge of the public works of the Ostrogothic kingdom (6th century), guaranteeing its survival. Einhard, Epistulae. Charlemagne's biographer uses Vitruvian vocabulary and concepts, reflecting the circulation of the text in the Carolingian Renaissance that produced the Codex Harleianus. 973

Book V — Public Buildings, Theater and Acoustics For the theory of the acoustic vessels of the theater (echea) and the harmonic arrangement of the seating, Vitruvius adapts the Greek musical theory of Aristoxenus of Tarentum (5.4-5.5), whose doctrine of tetrachords he explicitly summarizes. The design of the Greek theater compared to the Latin one (5.7) derives directly from Hellenic models. Book VI — Private Buildings and Climate The theory of the suitability of housing to latitudes and climates (6.1) is based on Greek ethnography and scientific geography, particularly on the Hippocratic tradition (On Airs, Waters and Places) and on Posidonius. Book VII — Finishes, stucco and painting His preface is the main source for reconstructing Vitruvius's library: it lists the Greek authors on proportions and machines. For stage perspective (scaenographia) he cites the works of Agatharchus of Samos and the commentaries of Democritus and Anaxagoras on optics (7.praef.11). Book VIII — Water The doctrine on the search, properties and conduction of water follows the Greek authors of natural sciences; Vitruvius invokes Thales (water as a principle) and gathers material from the Peripatetic and Hippocratic tradition on the qualities of waters (8.3). Book IX — Gnomonics and Astronomy The most dependent on Greek scientific sources. Vitruvius follows Berossus the Chaldean (who introduced astrology to Greece), Aristarchus of Samos (to whom he attributes the sundial and heliocentrism), Eudoxus of Cnidus, Eratosthenes (measurement of the meridian), and Archimedes (9.praef.; 9.1-9.8). The anecdote about the crown comes from the tradition surrounding Archimedes. 980

APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER Book X — Machines Vitruvian mechanics rests on the Alexandrian school. For pumps, the hydraulic organ, and the water-lifting machine, Vitruvius follows Ctesibius of Alexandria (10.7-10.8); for artillery and catapults, Philo of Byzantium and Ctesibius; for the lifting screw, Archimedes (10.6); and for siege engines, Diades (Alexander's engineer), Agesistratus, and the Hellenistic siegecraft tradition (10.13-10.16). Note. The works of these authors have been almost entirely lost; they are known primarily through Vitruvius himself, Pliny the Elder (Natural History), and the surviving Greek mechanical treatises (Heron of Alexandria, Philo). This appendix does not aim to be exhaustive, but rather to guide the reader towards the profound Hellenic roots of De architectura. 981

Critical editions of Vitruvius: overview and assessment The editions and translations that form the basis of the study of Vitruvius today are listed here in chronological order, along with a brief assessment of their usefulness. This list expands upon and formalizes what was presented in the Preliminary Note. Valentin Rose (Teubner, 1867; 2nd ed. 1899) An important modern critical edition of the Latin text, without a facing translation. Rose’s recension and apparatus remain valuable for comparison. In the present edition, Krohn (1912) is the declared reference text; a quotation following a different reading requires an explanation at its locus. Fritz Krohn (Teubner, 1912) Krohn’s critical edition is the declared reference text of this reading edition. It gives substantial weight to H while distinguishing the four principal witnesses H, S, E and G. Its constitution and apparatus should be compared with Rose and the relevant Budé volume at disputed passages, rather than reduced to a mechanical rule of following the oldest witness. Auguste Choisy (Paris, 1909) A bilingual Latin-French edition in four volumes, the work of an architect and construction historian. Without footnotes, it is notable for its introduction and its technical-construction approach; a precursor to editions geared towards architects. Frank Granger (Loeb, Harvard, 1931–1934) A two-volume bilingual Latin-English edition, based on the Harleianus. Convenient and accessible, but its translation and notes have aged and are now considered outdated in technical passages. Curt Fensterbusch (Darmstadt, 1964) Bilingual Latin-German edition with rigorous translation and notes; standard reference in the Germanic field for decades. 982

Edited by Pierre Gros, with contributions from Louis Callebat, Jean Soubiran, Philippe Fleury, and others, it offers one volume per book with critical text, French translation, introduction, and monographic commentary. APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER Appendix M · Stemma Codicum and the Manuscript Transmission This appendix sets out the genealogy of the surviving manuscripts of the De architectura, traces the principal stages of its transmission from Antiquity to the editio princeps, and explains the reasoning — the recensio — by which the two main branches of the tradition are reconstructed. The classification rests not on any single isolated error but on shared conjunctive errors (errores coniunctivi): when two or more codices preserve the same improbable corruption, a common ancestor may be inferred. 1. Chronology of the transmission (1st c. BC – 15th c. AD) c. 27–23 BCE — Composition. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio composes the ten books of the De architectura under Augustus, to whom the work is dedicated. It is the only complete treatise on architecture to survive from classical Antiquity. 1st–3rd c. CE — Ancient circulation. The work was transmitted through successive copies; the author’s autograph has not survived. The surviving witnesses do not establish when it was lost. Late Antiquity and the early Middle Ages — The text passed through copies that are now lost. Shared lacunae and textual disturbances allow editors to infer a common exemplar behind the surviving witnesses; neither its physical form nor an exact date is established by that inference alone. 6th–8th c. — The dark age of transmission. Documentation is extremely scarce. The survival of the De architectura through these centuries is one of the most remarkable episodes in the preservation of Roman literature. 9th c. — Carolingian Renaissance. Under Carolingian patronage, many ancient works were copied afresh. Harley MS 2767 (H) is an important early witness to De architectura. Its age and textual value do not establish that every surviving manuscript descends from it. Krohn distinguishes the H–S grouping from the Gudianus witnesses E and G; their relationships must be assessed through shared readings, corrections and losses. 10th–13th c. — Monastic and scholastic preservation. The work circulates in monastic libraries and cathedral schools. New copies appear; errors of 985

transcription, omissions and interpolations multiply, and some witnesses show contamination through the collation of different exemplars. 14th–15th c. — Humanist rediscovery. Italian scholars revive their interest in the technical literature of Antiquity; Poggio Bracciolini and others recover and diffuse dispersed manuscripts. Vitruvius becomes essential reading for Alberti, Francesco di Giorgio Martini and Leonardo da Vinci. Humanistic copies circulate widely. 1486 — Editio princeps. The first printed edition of the De architectura, published in Rome by Fra Giovanni Sulpicio da Veroli, marks the passage from manuscript to print and opens the modern editorial tradition. 2. General scheme of the transmission The surviving witnesses are commonly referred to a lost archetype, but the relationships between their branches must be stated according to a named critical edition. Krohn’s preface (1912, VIII) distinguishes H and S from E and G. The age and authority of H do not justify treating every other witness as its direct descendant. Lost common exemplar (Ω): inferred from shared lacunae and textual disturbance. H–S: Harleianus 2767 and Selestadiensis. E–G: Gudianus 132 and Gudianus 69. These paired witnesses summarize Krohn’s grouping; they do not assign direct descent to every copy. The manuscript tradition passes into print in the Roman editio princeps prepared by Giovanni Sulpicio da Veroli in the 1480s. 3. Stemma codicum of the De architectura The grouping is visualized in Figure 22 and cataloged in Table 9. The diagram reports H–S and E–G as distinguished by Krohn; it is not a complete stemma of all extant manuscripts. 4. Mechanisms of textual change and their stemmatic value The following examples illustrate how textual changes can arise. They are methodological examples, not reported readings assigned to named Vitruvian witnesses. A change acquires stemmatic significance only when its distribution, probability, and relation to contamination have been established from the apparatus or the manuscripts. I. Omission by homoeoteleuton. A scribe’s eye may pass between similar endings and omit the intervening text. A shared, unlikely omission may 986

APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER indicate common ancestry, provided independent recurrence and later correction have been considered. II. Dittography. A word or phrase may be copied twice. The same repetition in several witnesses can be significant, but a common copying error may also arise independently. III. Corruption of Greek terminology. An unfamiliar Greek expression may be altered, transliterated inconsistently, or replaced. Its evidential value depends on the precise reading and its distribution among identified witnesses. IV. Explanatory substitution. A technical expression may be replaced by a more familiar one. Such a substitution must be documented before it is attributed to a particular witness or branch. V. Transposition. Words, clauses, or larger units may change position. Shared unusual dislocations can be valuable evidence, particularly where they reveal the arrangement of an earlier exemplar. VI. Grammatical normalization. A copyist or editor may regularize an unfamiliar construction or spelling. An assimilated spelling is not inherently preferable to an unassimilated one, and common normalizations alone rarely establish a unique genealogy. VII. Numbers and proportions. Numerals, fractions, and dimensional signs are especially vulnerable in technical texts. Agreement must be assessed at a specific locus; a plausible reconstructed dimension does not independently establish the transmitted figure. VIII. Suppression of repetition. A passage judged redundant may be shortened. The editor must distinguish deliberate abbreviation from accidental omission and from an author’s own repetition. IX. Explanatory additions. A marginal or interlinear gloss may enter the running text. Its origin and date cannot be inferred from brackets alone; the relevant edition’s editorial signs must be read in context. 987

APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER aedis Augusti — V.1.7. Krohn’s printed passage describes the pronaos of a temple of Augustus beside the basilica; V.1.8 also mentions pronaum aedis and tribunal. The presence of Augustus in the edited text must be distinguished from an alleged omission by H, which is not established here. Neither an authorial second edition nor a Carolingian interpolation follows without further textual evidence. 2. The definition of the discipline — De architectura 1.1.1. Architecti est scientia — I.1.1. Krohn prints the genitive architecti. The sentence defines the architect’s body of knowledge, qualified by pluribus disciplinis et variis eruditionibus ornata. Its relation to the person of the architect matters to the argument; the abstract paraphrase ‘architecture is a science’ should not be substituted for a diplomatic quotation. fabrica — I.1.1. Krohn’s text defines fabrica as continuata ac trita usus meditatio. The term concerns sustained practical activity and must be read alongside ratiocinatio. A modern explanatory gloss is distinct from an attested medieval reading. ratiocinatione — I.1.1. Krohn prints ea nascitur ex fabrica et ratiocinatione. In the following definition, ratiocinatio explains and demonstrates what has been made through knowledge and reasoning. Reducing the term to numerical calculation alone would narrow its meaning; that semantic point does not establish the readings of H, G or later witnesses. 3. The Greek aesthetic vocabulary — De architectura 1.2.1. The Greek words suffered grave degradation in the manual transmission, since the Western medieval copyists of the Carolingian scriptoria did not know the Greek alphabet (Graeca sunt, non leguntur). τάξις — I.2.1. Krohn prints τάξις as the Greek counterpart of ordinatio. The explanatory discussion concerns order and the measured organization of the work. Claims about a blank in H, the form tasis in G, or a first restoration by Turnebus require separate documentary support and are not adopted as established variants here. διάθεσιν — I.2.1. Krohn prints this accusative form after hanc autem Graeci; the dictionary form is διάθεσις. The corresponding Latin term is dispositio. Vitruvius subsequently describes its ideae as plan, elevation and scenic representation. These are textual and conceptual observations, not proof of a particular corrupt reading in a named manuscript. 989

symmetria — I.2. The word concerns the commensurable relation of the parts to one another and to the whole through a common measure. It should not be reduced to bilateral symmetry. An anonymous scholium or the wording of a later manuscript cannot be treated as evidence without a source and location. 4. Pozzolana and the geology of concrete — De architectura 2.6.1. genus pulveris — II.6.1. Krohn prints Est etiam genus pulveris and locates the material in the districts around Vesuvius. Vitruvius describes its mixture with lime and aggregate and its hardening under water. This is a technical account of volcanic building material; the alleged variant arenae is not assigned to a manuscript family here. circa Vesuvium montem — II.6.1. The phrase locates the volcanic material geographically. The received historical dating of Vitruvius places the work before the eruption of 79 CE, but this phrase alone cannot prove that a later copyist or interpolator would necessarily have mentioned that eruption. 5. The figure of man and the genesis of proportion — De architectura 3.1.3. The well-proportioned body — III.1.1–3. Krohn’s text relates the design of temples to the proportional relations of a well-formed human body, hominis bene figurati. The circular and square constructions are both described in III.1.3. They should not be presented as a Renaissance addition to an otherwise non-geometrical ancient passage. item corporis centrum medium naturaliter est umbilicus — III.1.3. Krohn prints the navel as the center of the circle traced around the outstretched body. The same section then describes the square derived from height and arm span. Leonardo’s later distinction of centers belongs to the reception and graphic interpretation of the passage; it is not a textual conjecture in Vitruvius’s Latin. 990

APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER Appendix N · Restitutio vocabulorum Graecorum Vitruvius frequently uses Greek technical vocabulary, sometimes in Greek script and sometimes in Latinised forms. This glossary supplies lexical forms, equivalents and explanations. A Latin transliteration is not automatically a corruption, and a dictionary lemma need not be the inflected form printed in the treatise. The entries do not establish individual manuscript readings without an identified critical source. Appendix D provides selected page references. I. Aesthetic and modular concepts (Book I, chapter 2) 1. τάξις (taxis) Textual form: τάξις in Krohn, I.2.1. Restitution: τάξις (nominative singular, from τάσσω, ‘to set in order’, ‘to arrange in a row’). Vitruvian equivalent: ordinatio. Note: not to be confused with the mere placing of objects. In Aristotle and Hellenistic usage τάξις implies a mathematical and quantitative ordering. Vitruvius defines it as the measure of the members of a work in relation to the whole through the module (modulus): the establishment of the basic metric pattern. 2. διάθεσις (diathesis) Textual form: διάθεσιν, accusative singular, in Krohn, I.2.1. Restitution: διάθεσις (Vitruvius uses the accusative διάθεσιν; from διατίθημι, ‘to dispose’, ‘to arrange effectively’). Vitruvian equivalent: dispositio. Note: the expression of the τάξις in design. It is made visible through three modes of graphic representation (ideae): ichnographia (plan), orthographia (elevation) and scaenographia (perspective). 3. οἰκονομία (oikonomia) Textual form: οἰκονομία in Krohn, I.2.1; oeconomia is a Latin transliteration. Restitution: οἰκονομία (from οἶκος, ‘house’, and νόμος, ‘law, management’). 991

Vitruvian equivalent: distributio. Note: under Augustus the term carries a double, technical and financial nuance. It implies the prudent management of materials and budget (sumptus), but also the fitting of the building to the owner according to social status, and the pragmatic adaptation of the architecture to the local climate. 4. εὐρυθμία (eurythmia) Corrupt reading: eurithmia, euritmia (direct Latinisation). Lexical form: εὐρυθμία, with the prefix εὖ and the noun ῥυθμός, ‘rhythm’ or ‘ordered movement’. Note: a qualitative concept of visual perception. Whereas τάξις is purely mathematical and objective, εὐρυθμία is the aesthetic result perceptible to the human eye: the graceful and harmonious appearance of the whole when contemplated. 5. συμμετρία (symmetria) Latinised form: symmetria. The Greek lemma explains the technical vocabulary; variants such as simetria require an identified source before they can be assigned to a witness. Restitution: συμμετρία (from σύν, ‘with’, and μέτρον, ‘measure’). Note: a critical point for collation. In late and medieval Latin the term degraded semantically to ‘bilateral symmetry’. The following survey outlines the principal questions that continue to occupy specialists, so that the reader may situate the present edition within the living debate. On the text and its transmission. The editions of Valentin Rose (1867; 1899) and Fritz Krohn (1912) remain central to the constitution of the Latin text. Harley MS 2767 is the oldest known surviving copy and a witness of substantial authority. Krohn distinguishes H and S from E and G; the later witnesses cannot all be dismissed as a single contaminated group. The weight of each reading must be considered at its locus. On the date and unity of the work. The treatise is generally dated between 27 and 23 BCE and dedicated to Augustus. While some scholars have detected signs of stratified composition or later interpolation in particular passages, the substantial unity of the ten books is now broadly accepted. On the author’s identity. Almost nothing is known of Vitruvius’s life beyond what the prefaces disclose: military service under Caesar and a pension obtained through the mediation of Octavia. The cognomen Pollio rests on slender and late evidence, and the older identification of the author with Mamurra (proposed by Thielscher) is now generally rejected. On the foundational categories. The interpretation of ordinatio, dispositio, eurythmia, symmetria, decor, and distributio is a central crux. Following the commentary of Pierre Gros in the Budé edition and the philological studies of Louis Callebat, symmetria is now understood as commensurability—modular proportion—rather than modern bilateral symmetry. In the Anglophone sphere, the translation and commentary of Ingrid D. Rowland and Thomas Noble Howe (1999) and the work of Indra Kagis McEwen on the Vitruvian body have reframed much of the discussion. On the Greek sources and reception. Stemma codicum — the genealogical tree of the manuscripts, showing which copies depend on which and so which readings are likeliest to go back to Ω. Apparatus criticus — the band of notes printed beneath the Latin text recording the variant readings of the witnesses and the reasons for the editor’s choice; what may look like “mere grammar” is in fact the recovery of the original sense. Lectio difficilior potior — “the more difficult reading is the stronger”: between two readings the harder is the likelier original, since copyists tend to simplify an unfamiliar text — and Vitruvius’s technical Latin was often unfamiliar. Lectio facilior — the “easier” reading, frequently a later simplification or a fifteenth-century humanist “correction” that smoothed the grammar at the cost of authenticity. Contaminatio — the mixing of readings from two or more manuscript families in a single copy (as in the Selestadiensis), producing a hybrid text that the editor must disentangle. Crux desperationis (†) — the “cross of despair”, placed in the text where a passage is so corrupt that it cannot be restored with certainty — a mark of editorial honesty rather than of failure. The oldest codices and their history The transmission of De architectura rests almost entirely on the work of Carolingian copyists. When, around the year 800, the cultural renaissance fostered by Charlemagne and his teachers — Alcuin of York, Theodulf of Orléans — promoted the systematic copying of ancient authors, Vitruvius's treatise was one of the technical texts that escaped oblivion. The essential testimony of the entire tradition dates from that period. Theses on Vitruvius This chapter gathers, in concise form, the principal scholarly positions that underlie the present edition. They are offered as theses for discussion: where a statement rests on textual, archaeological, or philological evidence it is presented as such; where it belongs to the editor’s interpretive proposal, it is expressly marked as the author’s hypothesis and not as established consensus. The chapter is deliberately brief and may be expanded in subsequent editions. 1. A single complete witness, not the “first architect.” De architectura is not the earliest architecture ever written but the only complete treatise on the subject to survive from classical antiquity. Vitruvius’s historical importance lies in this completeness and in the systematic ambition of his ten books, not in any claim to have founded the discipline. The Greek treatises of Hermogenes, Pytheos and others that Vitruvius cites as his sources are lost; what survives of the ancient theory of building survives largely through him, so the claim this edition defends is one of transmission and completeness, not of priority. 2. The triad is a system, not a checklist. firmitas, utilitas, and venustas (De architectura 1.3.2) are neither optional nor separable. In Vitruvius’s conception, beauty arises from, and is inseparable from, sound construction and fitness for use; the same proportional reasoning that makes a building stand also makes it pleasing. Read in this way the three terms are not a checklist to be satisfied in turn but a single requirement seen from three sides, and the later reception that treated them as separable departs from Vitruvius’s own emphasis on their interdependence. 3. symmetria is modular commensurability, not modern symmetry. Vitruvian symmetria (συμμετρία) denotes the proportional correspondence of the parts to one another and to the whole through a common module; it must not be read as the modern, post-eighteenth-century notion of bilateral or mirror symmetry. The confusion is consequential, for rendering symmetria as “symmetry” imports a modern visual idea of balance that the Latin does not carry and obscures the modular reasoning — the use of a common module (modulus) — on which the whole proportional system rests. 1012

APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER 4. The homo bene figuratus is not the “Vitruvian Man.” Vitruvius (3.1) describes a well-proportioned human figure inscribed within circle and square as a canon of proportion; he does not give the celebrated phrase or image later associated with Leonardo. The Renaissance “Vitruvian Man” is an interpretive elaboration, not a quotation of the text. His concern is to derive the proportions of the temple from those of the well-formed body; the image of a single figure simultaneously inscribed in circle and square, with its famous shifting of centers, is Leonardo’s graphic solution to a problem the text poses but does not itself resolve. 5. Pythagorean number-symbolism is the author’s hypothesis. Vitruvius names Pythagoras and the practice of composing precepts in “cubes” of 216 verses (6³) in the preface to Book V; his use of number is technical. Any further reading of 216 or of the cube as a carrier of cosmic or sacred meaning is advanced here explicitly as the author’s interpretive proposal, not as Vitruvius’s stated intention. The distinction is methodological: the technical use of proportion is documented and defended philologically, whereas the symbolic resonance of particular numbers is offered as a separate and clearly labeled interpretive layer. 6. The transmission preserves collateral witnesses. The text descends through a complex medieval manuscript tradition in which the Carolingian Harleianus 2767 (H) is a major witness and Gudianus 69 (G) preserves an important collateral line. The Latin in this edition follows Krohn (1912), checked against Rose (1899) and the Budé volumes. Greek technical terminology, sometimes corrupted or transliterated in transmission, is normalized in the present text according to the critical editions and discussed in Appendix N and the Conspectus of Greek Terms. 7. The Basilica at Fano is the one work Vitruvius claims — and a current test case. The basilica at Fanum Fortunae is the building Vitruvius explicitly says he designed and supervised (5.1.6–10). On 19 January 2026 the Italian Ministry of Culture announced the identification of the remains in Piazza Andrea Costa as that basilica, and further archaeological investigation continued. Institutional identification, excavated evidence, the ancient measurements and modern 1013

Excursus · The Querelle of Proportion: Vitruvius, Palladio, and Perrault No question runs deeper through the reception of the De architectura than this one: are the proportions that Vitruvius records grounded in nature, and therefore binding upon every architect in every age, or are they conventions — beautiful because they are familiar, authoritative because they are old? On the answer hangs the whole status of Vitruvius’ canon. If proportion is a law of nature, the treatise is a body of science; if it is custom, the treatise is a record of taste. The debate came to a head in seventeenth-century France, but its terms are already latent in Vitruvius himself. Vitruvius grounds beauty in symmetria — the commensurability of every part with a fixed module — and derives that commensurability from the proportions of the well-formed human body (3.1) and, by analogy, from the consonances of music (5.4). For him the orders are not arbitrary: the Doric carries the proportions of a man, the Ionic those of a matron, the Corinthian those of a maiden (4.1). Proportion is thus a natural and quasi-mathematical fact, discovered rather than invented. Andrea Palladio (1508–1580) inherited this conviction and gave it its most influential modern form. In the I quattro libri dell’architettura (Venice, 1570) he prescribes seven “most beautiful” room-shapes whose ratios — the square, the diagonal of the square, and the simple musical proportions 2:3, 3:4, 3:5 — echo the harmonic intervals. For Palladio, as for Alberti before him (De re aedificatoria, 1452), the architect who follows these ratios does not impose a private preference but obeys a harmony written into the cosmos. This is the doctrine that Rudolf Wittkower named the “harmonic” or “musical” theory of proportion. Claude Perrault (1613–1688), physician, anatomist and member of the Académie des Sciences, also participated in the Louvre colonnade project. His French translation, Les dix livres d’architecture de Vitruve (Paris, 1673; revised 1684), brought together commentary and engraved illustrations. His criticism of proportional authority must be read in the context of that close engagement with the treatise. 1028

APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER In the preface to that translation, and at length in the Ordonnance des cinq espèces de colonnes selon la méthode des anciens (Paris, 1683), Perrault distinguished two kinds of architectural beauty. Positive beauty (beauté positive) rests on causes that convince everyone — richness of material, precision and cleanness of execution, bilateral regularity, and magnitude. Arbitrary beauty (beauté arbitraire), by contrast, comprises the proportions of the orders; these please us, Perrault argued, not because reason or nature compels them but because custom and association have accustomed the eye to them. There is no single ratio that nature dictates: the proof, he observed, is that the proportions admired by the ancients themselves vary from building to building and from author to author. From this premise Perrault drew a practical method as radical as his theory. Rather than seek the one true proportion, he proposed a mean or averaged system, derived by reconciling the divergent measures of the most admired ancient buildings into a simple, memorable rule. Proportion, for Perrault, was to be regulated by reasonable convention — by the architect’s judgment and the consensus of taste — not deduced from a law of nature. The challenge did not go unanswered. François Blondel (1618–1686), first director of the Académie Royale d’Architecture, defended the older view in his Cours d’architecture (1675–1683), insisting that proportion possesses an objective foundation in number, in music, and in nature, exactly as Vitruvius had taught. The exchange between Perrault and Blondel became the architectural front of the wider querelle des anciens et des modernes: Blondel for the ancients and the absolute, Perrault for the moderns and the conventional. The quarrel was never settled, and that is its importance. It exposed, once and for all, that the Vitruvian canon can be read in two incompatible ways, and that a reader must choose. Later theory has oscillated between the poles. The harmonic tradition revived in the proportional systems of the nineteenth century and in Le Corbusier’s Modulor (1948), which sought once more to anchor design in the measures of the body; the conventionalist tradition fed the historicism and, ultimately, the proportional skepticism of much modern practice. For the present edition the controversy carries a precise consequence. When Vitruvius states that a column shall be of such-and-such a diameter, or that the 1029

eustyle intercolumniation shall measure two and a quarter diameters, the modern reader is entitled to ask whether such figures record a discovered law or a codified habit. This edition takes no side in the metaphysical question. It renders the proportions faithfully, as Vitruvius gives them, and leaves to the architect — as Perrault would have wished, and as Palladio would have resisted — the freedom to regard them either as nature’s rule or as the accumulated wisdom of a tradition. The text is law for those who read it as law, and counsel for those who read it as counsel. Select references. The Fano basilica: the case of direct verification The basilica of Fanum Fortunae is the only building Vitruvius claims to have designed and supervised himself (conlocavi curavique faciendam, 5.1.6), and so it offers an exceptional test of the text against material remains. In January 2026 the Italian authorities (the Marche Region, the Municipality of Fano and the Soprintendenza) announced the identification, in Piazza Andrea Costa at Fano, of the remains of a monumental basilica attributed to this work. EPILOGUE The figure of Vitruvius presents a paradox characteristic of many foundational authors: while we know remarkably little about his life, his De architectura has shaped architectural thought for more than two thousand years. This disproportion between the obscurity of the author and the enduring legacy of his work is not accidental: it is the very nature of foundational texts, which survive precisely because they cease to belong to their author and become the heritage of their readers. Vitruvius’s treatise has come down to us mutilated, deprived of its original figures. The illustrations that accompanied the text — the diagrams of the orders, the plans of the temples, the layouts of the machines — were lost somewhere in the chain of copies, and the Renaissance had to reconstruct them with ruler and compass from the words alone. This loss, far from impoverishing the work, made it fruitful: it forced Alberti, Cesariano, Palladio, and Barbaro to read Vitruvius with pencil in hand, transforming philology into a project and commentary into architecture. If this journey through the Ten Books teaches us anything, it is that the triad Vitruvius enunciated — firmitas, utilitas, venustas — does not describe three separable qualities, but rather three facets of the same measure. Solidity without utility is premature ruin; utility without beauty, mere construction; beauty without solidity, ephemeral scenery. For Vitruvius, architecture begins where the three converge, and this conviction — that number, matter, and form obey a single reason — remains the core of any architectural theory worthy of the name. This edition has sought to uphold a twofold commitment: historical and philological rigor, on the one hand, and openness to the symbolic dimension of the treatise, on the other, always maintaining the distinction between what the sources allow us to affirm and what belongs to the author's interpretation. Perhaps this is the most faithful way to honor Vitruvius, who wrote convinced that the architect should master both the square and astronomy, construction and reasoning, the hand and number. A debt and a hope remain. Every edition of a classical work is provisional: further collation, closer translation and a more precise apparatus can always 1040
